5-6 
DEVELOPING AN EFFECTIVE COOLING WATER TREATMENT 
PROGRAM. 
An effective and complete cooling water treatment program addresses many factors, 
including those associated with compliance and safety, protection of equipment, and 
cost. Compliance and safety considerations are mandatory components of the program. 
Achieving or exceeding minimally acceptable equipment protection at the lowest 
possible cost is an advisable outcome for a well-designed program. The overall cost of 
the treatment program includes not only the cost of chemical treatment, but also the 
costs of water, disposal, manpower, and equipment. Development of an appropriate 
cooling water treatment program is dependent upon knowledge of both the specific 
equipment to be protected and the quality of the water to be used (source water and 
system water). 
 
 

=== PDF Page 154 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
137 
5-6.1 
Equipment. 
Corrosion inhibitors are selected based on the metallurgy of individual pieces of cooling 
system equipment. Typical systems include equipment components of different metals. 
For example, systems may include smooth and enhanced copper tube bundles, mild 
steel transfer piping, and galvanized cooling tower components; therefore, to select the 
proper corrosion inhibitor, it is important to identify all metals contacted by the cooling 
water. (See Table 5-10 for corrosion inhibitor selection criteria.) 
5-6.2 
Operational Features and Parameters. 
Operational features and parameters of the cooling water system must be known to 
select the proper scale and deposit inhibitors. This requirement refers to operational 
parameters such as maximum temperature, minimum velocities, usage patterns, and 
whether or not layup periods occur. The best chemical treatment programs cannot 
overcome the stresses of poorly operated systems. A good example of system stress is 
intermittent chiller operation that allows for SS accumulation (deposits) in chiller tube 
surfaces due to low flow or lack of flow. This situation creates a strong potential for 
under-deposit corrosion and for MIC that the chemical treatment may not be able to 
overcome completely. Stagnant water can also cause deposits and corrosion. High 
water temperatures can cause scale. The maximum water temperature should be 
known so that the proper scale-control method can be used. 
5-6.3 
Water Quality. 
Water quality within the cooling water system is a critical consideration. The source may 
be potable or reuse or recycled water. The various water constituents must be known so 
appropriate water treatment chemicals can be selected for controlling specific water 
quality parameters. 
5-6.4 
Cooling Water Treatment Programs. 
5-6.4.1 
Categories. 
For the purpose of developing a water treatment program, cooling tower recirculating 
water systems can be divided into three basic categories: 
• 
Small-sized towers – capacity less than 25 tons (88 kilowatts) 
• 
Medium-sized towers – 25 to 100 tons (88 to 352 kilowatts) 
• 
Large-sized towers - greater than 100 tons (352 kilowatts) 
The water treatment program selected for cooling tower systems will vary depending on 
the size of the tower (among other factors). Treatment program considerations are 
described in paragraphs 5-6.5 and 5-6.6 for small-, medium-, and large-sized towers, 
respectively. 
 
 

=== PDF Page 155 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
138 
5-6.4.2 
Cycles of Concentration (COC). 
The COC of small, medium, and large cooling towers may be controlled by blowdown, 
either automatic or manual, to avoid the high levels of silica and calcium salts that can 
lead to scale. If the cooling tower is not chemically treated, the COC should be adjusted 
to be slightly less than the lowest allowable COC value based on all scale-forming water 
ingredients (see paragraph 5- 3.3). The use of chemical treatment permits a higher 
COC, which is usually limited by either the chemical effectiveness or the water 
treatment control. 
EXAMPLE: An untreated cooling tower system can operate at 10 COC based on the 
level of silica without scale forming, but can operate at only 2 COC based on the level of 
calcium carbonate. Accordingly, the tower system should be operated at a maximum of 
2 COC. The system can likely be operated at 5 to 6 COC when an effective chemical 
treatment is applied and maintained to control calcium carbonate. 
5-6.5 
Treatment Program for Small Cooling Towers. 
Typically a small cooling tower will have a rating of less than 25 tons (88 kilowatts). The 
treatment program used for small towers should be designed to be simple to control and 
easy to apply, with very little operator attention required. This does not mean that no 
attention is required, only less than that required for medium-sized systems. The 
treatment program for small systems is shown in Table 5-12. 
Table 5-12 Small Cooling Tower Treatment Program 
Parameter 
Method 
COC 
Do not exceed COC limits for untreated water 
Scale and corrosion program 
Dry, slowly soluble, phosphate compound 
Microbiological program 
Dry, slowly soluble, oxidizing biocide 
SS 
Filtration and periodic wash downs, as required 
5-6.5.1 
Treatment. 
Small systems can be treated with a low dosage (5 to 10 ppm) of a slowly soluble 
phosphate chemical (sodium/calcium polyphosphate) by placing a nylon mesh bag 
containing the product into the cooling tower. The product, if applied in this manner, will 
usually provide adequate scale and corrosion control. Microbiological control can be 
obtained by use of a dry, pelletized, oxidizing biocide, such as bromo- chlorohydantoin 
or isocyanuric acid plus sodium bromide (see paragraph 5-4.4.1). 

=== PDF Page 156 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
139 
Either of these biocides can be fed continuously via a feeder or suspended in a mesh 
bag in the cooling tower water. The cooling tower sump should be kept clean of SS and 
other debris by use of a filter and periodic wash downs. 
5-6.6 
Treatment Program for Medium and Large Cooling Towers. 
The chemical treatment program for these cooling tower systems (typically greater than 
25 tons [88 kilowatts]) requires sufficient, regular testing as well as water and chemical 
control to protect the equipment in contact with the cooling water. Usually treatment 
includes control of scale, fouling, microbiological growth, and corrosion. The 
composition of an optimum chemical treatment program for cooling towers on a military 
installation depends on the quality of water available, the operating conditions of the 
cooling system, and the environmental constraints placed on treatment chemicals in the 
blowdown water (effluent discharge limitations). Conditions at a particular installation 
may require variation of the quantity or mix of the chemicals suggested in Table 5-13. 
Table 5-13 Treatment Programs for Medium and Large Cooling Towers. 
Parameter 
Approach 
COC 
Target a minimum of 3 COC (ideally 5 COC) that the chemical 
treatment will allow. 
Corrosion control 
1. Use of cathodic corrosion, possibly supplemented with 
anodic inhibitors for mild steel. If a galvanized cooling 
tower is present, use a polysilicate or low-level 
phosphate while keeping pH in the range of 8 to 9. 
2. Copper corrosion inhibitor should be used for all copper 
tubes and especially for enhanced and super-enhanced 
copper tubing. 
Scale control 
Phosphonate/polymer program, augmented by a phosphate 
dispersant if phosphate corrosion inhibitor is used. 
SS 
Polymer dispersant coupled with adequate flow. Avoid no- flow 
conditions in heat exchangers as much as possible. 
Mechanical filtration and routine physical sump cleaning 
recommended. 
Microbiological control 
1. Primary biocide: oxidizing biocide using continuous feed 
or slug feed as an alternate. 
2. Secondary biocide: non-oxidizing biocide using slug feed, 
as required. 
 
 
 

=== PDF Page 157 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
140 
5-6.6.1 
Treatment. 
Medium and large cooling towers are usually, but not always, treated with a liquid 
formulation containing both scale inhibitors and corrosion inhibitors. These are often 
simply referred to as an "inhibitor.” Inhibitor products are usually fed on a continuous 
basis using automated control and feed equipment. The concentration of these 
formulated products varies greatly from vendor to vendor. Biocides are usually, but not 
always, liquid products. It is common to use an oxidizing biocide as a primary biocide 
and a non-oxidizing biocide as a secondary biocide, used as needed to control bacteria 
and other biological growth. Oxidizing biocides can either be fed continuously at a low 
level or dosed periodically at a higher level. Non-oxidizers are dosed as needed and 
only when oxidizing biocides are either ineffective or not used at all. 
5-6.6.2 
Testing. 
Testing should be done regularly to insure that COC, chemical levels, and bacteria 
levels are within the targeted control range. This requirement could demand a testing 
frequency of three times per week, or even daily. 
5-6.7 
Cooling Tower Operator Duties. 
If detected early, problems associated with scaling, corrosion and fouling in a cooling 
tower system can be minimized by corrective action. Some of the things the operator 
should look for when on-site are described below. 
5-6.7.1 
Cooling Tower Distribution Deck. 
It is important to look for the presence of algae, debris, or anything that has plugged 
water distribution holes causing an uneven water flow through the tower, thus lowering 
tower efficiency. Clean plugged holes and replace damaged water distribution spray 
nozzles. In addition, look for the presence of algae deposits. If algae deposits are 
present, increase the level or frequency of biocide or algaecide treatment, and cover the 
deck if uncovered. 
5-6.7.2 
Cooling Tower Fill, Air Intake Slats, and Basin. 
5-6.7.2.1 
Scale Deposits on Cooling Tower Fill. 
The presence of deposits, particularly on cooling tower fill, can be established by 
removing some fill to determine if partial plugging has occurred. Scale can range in 
color from white to gray or reddish depending on the scale composition. Scale formation 
on the cooling tower fill usually indicates a severe scaling situation. If possible, obtain a 
sample of the scale for analysis and, based on the result, select a scale inhibitor for that 
specific scale. 
 
 

=== PDF Page 158 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
141 
5-6.7.2.2 
Scale Deposits on Air Intake Slats. 
Scale can form on the air intake slats of a cooling tower. This buildup is due mostly to 
water splashing and evaporating, causing deposition of soluble salts or minerals. This

11-3 
DEVELOPING A SCOPE OF WORK (SOW) FOR INDUSTRIAL WATER 
TREATMENT. 
This paragraph applies only to paragraph 11-2.1.3. A SOW (sometimes called a 
“statement of work” or a “statement of services to be provided”) is developed for 
inclusion in the required procurement documents (request for proposal/bid (RFP/RFB) 
and contract). The SOW will identify the specific services, chemicals, and equipment 
that a contractor is to provide under the terms of the contract. The SOW will, at a 
minimum, specify or identify the following: SOW to be performed; qualifications of 
supplier; water characteristics of each system to be treated; description of industrial 
water systems and their operation; performance specification (results required); service 
requirements; equipment requirements for control, feed, monitoring, and sampling; 
requirements for chemicals and test equipment; and quotation for total chemical cost 
and usage. These issues are described below. 
11-3.1 
Qualifications. 
The SOW specifies the minimum qualification requirements for contractors and 
contractor representatives. These requirements are developed to allow the participation 
of qualified contractors (water treatment chemical companies) having national, regional, 
and local operations. The SOW can specify the minimum number of years that the 
company has been in business and the minimum number of years and type of 
experience of contractor representatives, as well as required technical service 
capabilities. 
11-3.2 
Submittal Requirements and Format. 
The SOW clearly specifies the type of response (submittal) that is required from an RFP 
or RFB. This is necessary to avoid receiving bid responses that are so different in their 
presentation that they cannot be easily or objectively compared. The evaluation process 
can be simplified by requiring bidders to provide a comprehensive acknowledgement 
that they understand and accept all requirements for compliance, qualifications, service 
requirements, and performance standards. The RFP/RFB should require a simple, 
generic, technical summary that lists the proposed chemical technology and treatment 
ranges for each type of system to be serviced under the procurement. 
11-3.3 
Water Quality. 
The water supplied as makeup to industrial water systems is characterized in terms of 
its source, treatment, and quality, including seasonal and temporal variances. If external 
treatment is used on individual systems such as a steam boiler, this treatment is 
identified. 
11-3.4 
Description of Systems and Operations. 
A description of the number, capacity, and types of systems to be serviced under the 
contract is a critically important element of a SOW. The metallurgy of all water-
contacted surfaces is identified. Without this information, performance standards cannot 

=== PDF Page 220 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
203 
be adequately defined. The condition of equipment is documented. Operational 
parameters, such as the equipment duty, load, and usage, are described so that water 
usage (preferably total water usage for each system) and chemical restrictions can be 
considered in developing the proposal. 
11-3.5 
Performance Specification. 
Performance criteria are specified for protecting equipment against deposition, 
corrosion, and biological growths. Certain minimally acceptable standards for 
performance must be met. Recommended or example performance standards are listed 
in Chapters 4, 5 and 6 for the respective types of industrial water systems. Allowances 
are made for problems that cannot be totally controlled by chemical treatment alone. 
One example is SS accumulation in a cooling tower system. Chemical dispersants can 
aid in keeping SS from settling on metal surfaces, but it may require adequate flow and 
physical removal to maintain good control. 
11-3.6 
Service Requirements. 
The SOW accurately describes the services to be provided by the contractor. Service 
includes the frequency of on-site visits, the duties to be performed, and the methods of 
reporting. The duties to be performed can include these activities: water testing; making 
log entries; training; maintaining automated chemical control and feed equipment; 
manual addition of chemicals to industrial water systems; inventory control; corrosion 
coupon studies; microbiological population determination; equipment inspections; 
laboratory support; quarterly reviews; and annual reviews. 
11-3.7 
Control, Feed, Monitoring and Sampling Equipment Requirements. 
The SOW specifies what equipment, if any, is required to achieve consistent control of 
the makeup water treatment chemical program. Automated control and feed equipment 
is required on most medium and large cooling towers and on most steam boilers. 
Automated control and feed equipment helps limit the demand for service maintenance. 
To provide for the preparation of an appropriate SOW, engineering and facility 
maintenance personnel carefully evaluate their capabilities in the area of water 
treatment and water systems. Inadequate water treatment equipment can result in 
higher service requirements or inconsistent control of the chemical program. 
Descriptions of chemical applications can be found in Chapter 8. 
11-3.8 
Chemicals and Test Equipment. 
The SOW specifies any restrictions on the use or discharge of chemicals. Examples of 
restrictions can include limitations on the use of acid, shipping container size limits, 
microbiocide selection criteria, and limitation on use of dry chemicals. 
The SOW specifies how the cost of chemicals and services is being calculated and 
quoted. For example, quotations for chemical treatment can be based on the cost to 
treat 133.666 cubic feet (3.785 cubic meters) of water. Cost for services in the SOW can 
be required to be included in the cost of chemical treatment or quoted separately as line 

=== PDF Page 221 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
204 
items, time, and materials. Contracts that require a "not-to- exceed" quotation supply 
bidders with a not-to-exceed water usage estimate. 
11-4 
REPORTS AND AUDITS. 
Reports and audits are tools for documenting performance and cost effectiveness of 
any industrial water treatment program. Audits serve to verify results from the water 
treatment service company. Audits also serve to verify the cost-effectiveness of product 
being supplied by the water treatment service company. Audits are performed by 
qualified agencies within the military branch in question or by independent consultants 
contracted to perform such duties. 
 

=== PDF Page 222 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
205 
APPENDIX A PRACTICAL (PUCKORIUS) SCALING INDEX (PSI) 
A-1 
DEVELOPMENT OF PSI. 
Have been used to predict the tendency of water to form or dissolve scale. Both the LSI 
and the RSI are based on the pH of saturation (pHs) for calcium carbonate under a 
specific water condition. Both indices use the measured pH of the cooling water. 
1. LSI = (measured pH) - (pHs). A positive value indicates scale; a negative 
value indicates no scale. 
2. RSI = (2 pHs) - (measured pH). A value below 6 means scale; above 6 
means no scale. 
A-1.1 
PSI. 
Use of LSI and RSI sometimes gave inconsistent or even conflicting results. Based on a 
long-term study relative to calcium carbonate scale formation when applying both the 
LSI and RSI, P.R. Puckorius and J.M. Brooke developed a new index that gives much 
better and more consistent indication of cooling water-scaling conditions. The new 
index, the Practical Scaling Index (PSI), sometimes called the Puckorius Scaling Index, 
is based on correcting the system pH to match the total alkalinity of the water being 
evaluated. This is necessary because the pH is often buffered, causing the pH to relate 
incorrectly to the bicarbonate alkalinity, one of the factors in the pHs calculation. 
A-2 
CALCULATING PSI. 
To calculate the PSI, the pHs is determined in the same manner as for the LSI and RSI. 
An adjusted or equilibrium pH (pHeq) is obtained from a total alkalinity/pH chart (Table 
A-7). The value of pHeq rather than measured pH is used in the following formula: 
PPPPPP = (22 ppppss) − (ppppeeee) 
A value below 6 means scale; above 6 means no scale. 
A-2.1 
Calculating pHs. 
The pHs can be determined from the relationship between various characteristics of 
water. The following factors and formula are used in determining the pHs: 
a. Factors needed to calculate pHs : 
A = TDS (ppm) (Table A-1) 
B = Temperature (°F) (Table A-2) 
C = Calcium hardness (ppm as CaCO3) (Table A-3) 
D = Total alkalinity (ppm as CaCO3) (Tables A-5 and A-6)

APPENDIX B CORROSION TESTING WITH COUPON-TYPE TEST 
SPECIMENS 
B-1 
PURPOSE. 
Corrosion tests with metal coupon test specimens are used to determine how corrosive 
water is to a specific metal. Coupon test specimens are particularly useful in monitoring 
the effectiveness of chemical corrosion control programs. The extent of both general 
and localized corrosion can be determined. Also, examination of the specimens as they 
are removed from the system can provide information regarding deposit accumulation 
or microbiological slime growth. Corrosion test coupons are usually used as corrosion 
test specimens for open and closed cooling systems, closed hot water systems, and 
domestic water systems. See ASTM Standard Test Method: Corrosivity of Water in the 
Absence of Heat Transfer (Weight Loss Methods), D2688-15e1. 
B-2 
APPLICATION. 
B-2.1 
Description of Coupons. 
The coupons are metal tags of various sizes. Generally, low-carbon steel specimens 
are used as the most susceptible metal to corrosion; however, copper, stainless steel, 
brass, and other metals are available for special studies. The specimens are prepared 
and cleaned to ensure uniformity and weighed. The general corrosion rate is 
determined after exposure. Coupons are cleaned and re-weighed. Corrosion rates are 
calculated based on the weight loss, time of exposure, and the area and specific gravity 
of the coupon, and are expressed in mils per year (MPY). 
B-2.2 
Test Conditions. 
Since the goal of the corrosion testing program is to provide information regarding 
conditions within the system, the corrosion coupons should be exposed to conditions 
that reflect those in the system as a whole. Water velocity and temperature will 
significantly affect the corrosion rate. Corrosion rates can be significantly increased 
when velocity is either too low or too high. For best results, water velocity flowing by the 
test specimen should be 3 to 5 feet per second (0.90 to 1.5 meters per second), and 
both adjustable and measurable. Temperature also affects the rate of corrosion, with 
higher temperatures usually increasing corrosion; therefore, in cooling water systems 
both the cold supply water and the hot return water should be evaluated with corrosion 
coupons. When only one test rack can be installed, the warm water return at the tower 
should be used to provide an average hot water temperature.

P00: DC-02 Mechanical Design Criteria Memorandum - Condenser Water Heat Rejection
P01: Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 3, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
This memorandum supersedes DC-02 Revision 2 in its entirety. Revision 3 adds the life-cycle cost objective (paragraph 4, EC-01) and the LifeCycleCost sheet of Appendix A.2.
P02: 1. Scope
P03: This memorandum states the criteria, conventions and deliverable requirements for the replacement of the condenser water heat rejection plants serving the Courthouse Central Utility Plant (CUP), the Data Annex (ANNEX) and the Laboratory Wing (LAB). The chillers, the condenser water pumps' hydraulic circuits and the electrical distribution are existing or already procured and are not in the scope of this design.
P04: 2. Adopted criteria
P05: 3. Plants and served loads
P06: Block cooling loads as a function of outdoor dry-bulb temperature are scheduled on M-603. Chiller performance data and condenser water limits are on M-601 and submittal VD-03.
P07: 4. Objective
P08: Each plant must be designed for the HIGHEST LIFE-CYCLE NET SAVINGS, relative to the basic design, consistent with every requirement of the adopted criteria and of this memorandum, with the life-cycle cost analysis performed as EC-01 directs under 10 CFR Part 436 Subpart A. It is not the design with the lowest energy, nor the one with the lowest first cost, unless the analysis makes it so.
P09: Annual plant electrical energy - the energy quantity the analysis prices - is the sum over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 of the bin hours multiplied by the coincident electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps of that plant.
P10: 5. Climatic and property basis
P11: 5.1 Governing station
P12: The climatic basis is the National Centers for Environmental Information Local Climatological Data record of the airport station serving the site, for the three complete calendar years in the project library. That record is the period of record (POR) for every percentile in this memorandum. Only observations whose report type is FM-15 or FM-16 are counted; the daily and monthly summary rows of the record are not observations. Records for any other station in the library are not part of the POR.
P13: 5.2 Design outdoor conditions
P14: A percentile design value is the value that was exceeded that percentage of the observations over the entire POR, taken as a single annual population (not a seasonal one). The design outdoor wet-bulb temperature for the heat rejection equipment is the 1.0 percent annual wet-bulb temperature so computed, adjusted as the adopted HVAC criteria require for open cooling towers. The failure-case calculation of paragraph 6.3 uses the wet-bulb basis that the adopted agency facilities standard prescribes for evaporative machines, adjusted the same way. Do not take design values from the cancelled weather-data criteria document.
P15: 5.3 Scenario bins
P16: Annual performance is evaluated on scenario bins formed from the POR observations: bin each observation by wet-bulb temperature in 2 deg F bins and by dry-bulb temperature in 5 deg F bins, take the bin condition as the bin mid-points, and scale the bin counts so that the bins total 8760 hours per year. The block load of a bin is the M-603 load at the bin dry-bulb temperature. Where a bin's dry-bulb mid-point would fall below its wet-bulb mid-point, the dry-bulb temperature is taken equal to the wet-bulb mid-point. The bin edges fall at whole multiples of the bin width measured from zero deg F: an observation belongs to the bin whose lower edge is the largest such multiple that does not exceed it, the lower edge belonging to the bin and the upper edge to the next one, so that a bin's mid-point is its lower edge plus half the bin width.
P17: 5.4 Freeze protection
P18: A basin heater and heat-traced makeup piping are required only where the 99.6 percent annual dry-bulb temperature computed from the POR is at or below 32 deg F. The design basis must state the computed 99.6 percent dry-bulb temperature and the determination that follows from it.
P19: 5.5 Property basis
P20: Moist air properties are those of the psychrometric routines of the reference implementation in the project library (saturation pressure over water, humidity ratio from dry- and wet-bulb, moist air enthalpy and density, and saturation temperature from enthalpy). The barometric pressure is the mean station pressure of the governing POR, not a sea-level or a standard-atmosphere value. Water is taken at 8.33 lb/gal and 1.0 BTU/lb-deg F, so that heat rejection in BTU/h is 500 times the flow in gpm times the range in deg F.
P21: 6. Plant configuration and operating conventions
P22: 6.1 Cells and controls
P23: All cells of a plant are of one model and one size and carry identical fan, motor, drift eliminator and material selections. Every tower fan motor is driven by a variable frequency drive. The number of cells must be a whole multiple of the number of chillers served.
P24: 6.2 Condenser water flow
P25: Each chiller has a dedicated constant-speed condenser water pump. The scheduled design flow is the flow with every chiller running; the flow with n chillers running is n/N of it. The per-chiller flow must lie inside the condenser flow limits of submittal VD-03 and the per-cell flow inside the limits of submittal VD-01.
P26: 6.3 Redundancy
P27: The plant must meet its design block load with the largest single cell out of service, at the failure-case wet-bulb basis of paragraph 5.2, with the remaining cells at full fan speed, and at an entering condenser water temperature no warmer than the machines' published maximum (submittal VD-03). This is the cooling robustness performance tier the agency facilities standard requires.
P28: With a cell out of service the design condenser water flow is unchanged - every chiller is still running on its dedicated constant-speed pump (paragraph 6.2) - and it is carried by the cells that remain in service. The flow through each remaining cell in that state must lie inside the per-cell flow limits of submittal VD-01 and inside the water flow rate ratio limits of the performance object (paragraph 6.8). A plant whose remaining cells would have to pass more than that does not meet this requirement, whatever temperature a calculation extrapolated beyond those limits might predict: a cell above its rated distribution capacity and outside the validity envelope of its performance model has no substantiated capability. The clamping described in the second part of paragraph 6.8 applies to the inlet wet-bulb temperature only; it does not apply to the water flow rate ratio, in this case or any other.
P29: 6.4 Condenser water pump power
P30: Condenser water pump total head is taken as a fixed static lift plus a friction component that varies with the square of the flow ratio:
P31:     H = H_static + (H_pipe + H_condenser) x (Q / Q_ref)^2        [ft of water]
P32:     Pump shaft power = Q x H / (3960 x eta_pump)                 [hp, Q in gpm]
P33:     Pump electrical input = shaft power x 0.7457 / eta_motor     [kW]
P34: where Q is the flow through one pump. The per-plant constants are:
P35: 6.5 Chiller staging
P36: Chillers stage on in order: the smallest number of machines whose available capacity at the operating leaving chilled water and entering condenser water temperatures meets the block load runs, and the load is divided equally between them.
P37: Available capacity here is the capacity the adopted performance data set makes available at those temperatures: the machine's reference capacity multiplied by its capacity-as-a-function-of-temperature curve evaluated at the operating point, and nothing else. The maximum part load ratio is not part of available capacity. It is a separate published limit - the ceiling on the load a machine that is already running may be given - and it is not applied to the capacity that decides how many machines run.
P38: 6.6 Cell staging
P39: Condenser water is distributed to every installed cell unless the resulting per-cell flow would fall below the effective minimum, which is the larger of the submittal's minimum per-cell flow and the flow at which the performance object's minimum water flow rate ratio is reached. Cells are then isolated one at a time until the per-cell flow is at or above the effective minimum. Tower fans of the cells in service modulate together.
P40: 6.7 Condenser water supply temperature control
P41: The condenser water supply temperature setpoint is scheduled as a wet-bulb-following reset: the setpoint is the larger of a scheduled floor and the outdoor wet-bulb temperature plus a scheduled offset, and is in no case below the minimum entering condenser water temperature the chillers are rated for. The fans modulate to the setpoint exactly as the reference implementation models a variable speed tower: full speed when the setpoint cannot be met, free convection when the fans are not needed, minimum speed with cycling below that. A condenser water bypass valve holds the setpoint when the tower would otherwise overcool, so the supply temperature never falls below the setpoint.
P42: 6.8 Validity of the performance correlation
P43: A cell may not be operated at a water flow rate ratio outside the limits stated in the performance object, because the implementation clamps the ratio there and the capability would not be substantiated. The range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits of the same object apply at every scenario. A design that operates outside them is not accepted.
P44: The inlet air wet-bulb temperature is treated differently, and deliberately. The reference implementation clamps it to the object's stated range before evaluating the correlation, so an outdoor wet bulb at or above the object's maximum is evaluated AT that maximum and is never extrapolated. The design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 lands on that maximum at this site. That is not an error and no work-around is required: it is what the adopted simulation basis does, and the wet-bulb limit is therefore not one of the envelope limits this paragraph tests.
P45: 6.9 Design point
P46: At the design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 and the design block load, with every chiller running at the scheduled design flow and the cells in service at full fan speed, the cells must deliver condenser water no warmer than the scheduled design supply temperature (CWSDESIGN), and the chillers must carry the design block load at that entering condenser water temperature. The validity limits of paragraph 6.8 - the water flow rate ratio limits, and the range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits - apply at this design point as they do at every scenario. A schedule may be conservative: a CWSDESIGN warmer than the selected cells actually need is acceptable.
P47: 6.10 Peak coincident demand
P48: The peak coincident electrical demand of a plant is the largest total electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps operating together, taken over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 and over nothing else. It is a maximum over those bins, not a design-day figure: neither the design point of paragraph 6.9 nor the redundancy case of paragraph 6.3 is a scenario bin - they are sizing conditions - and neither enters this maximum. Basin heaters, controls and lighting are not part of it. This is the quantity the motor control centre's spare capacity limits and the quantity the calculation workbook reports.
P49: 7. Water
P50: The water balance, the cycles of concentration and the treatment programme are governed by the adopted water treatment manual and by the reclaimed water correspondence and treatment memorandum in the project library.
P51: Two evaporation formulations are adopted for this project, and they are these two, named so that the choice is between two fully specified methods:
P52:   SATURATED-EXIT - the moist-air method of the reference implementation's tower water-use routine: the outlet air is saturated at the inlet enthalpy plus the water-side heat transfer divided by the air mass flow, and the evaporated mass is the air mass flow times the rise in specific humidity, converted to a volume with the density of water. As the routine computes them, the inlet enthalpy is that of saturated air at the inlet wet-bulb temperature, and the water density is taken at the mean of the inlet dry-bulb and the saturated outlet air temperatures, not below 4 deg C. The routine reads that density from fluid property tables that are not part of the shipped source; on this project it is taken as rho = 1000 x (1 - (T + 288.9414) / (508929.2 x (T + 68.12963)) x (T - 3.9863)^2) kg/m3, T in deg C. Every other quantity the method needs is in the shipped source and its header.
P53:   LOSS-FACTOR - the rule of thumb of the adopted water treatment manual's cooling tower chapter, with the constant and the temperature basis that chapter states and its own worked example confirms. It is NOT the reference implementation's user-factor path: that path reads a loss factor from an input field this project does not set, and the input dictionary that would supply a default for it is not part of the adopted basis.
P54: Either may be used. The design basis must state which one was used, and the water balance of the submitted workbook must be computed consistently with the stated choice throughout.
P55: 8. Deliverable
P56: For each plant P in {CUP, ANNEX, LAB} deliver CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf and CT_CALC_P.xlsx, and once for the package constraint_register.csv and design_basis.md. Appendix A fixes the formats.
P57: 9. Design basis content
P58: The design basis must state, for each plant, the governing constraint on the design in the form:
P59:     GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <plant>: <name> (relative margin <value>)
P60: where <name> is exactly one of the following six, and is the one with the smallest relative margin at the submitted design, and <value> is that relative margin:
P61: The six names above are the only admissible values of <name>. Where two of them are within 0.004 of each other at the submitted design, either may be stated.
P62: The margins are judged against the quantities the calculation workbook reports, not against a figure to a precision the workbook cannot carry. A relative margin is a small difference divided by a limit, so it is far more sensitive than the quantity it is computed from: near a limit, a 1 percent difference in peak demand can move the margin by more than half its value. The stated margin is therefore accepted when it agrees, within 0.004, with the margin computed from the workbook's own reported peak coincident demand, annual makeup and design supply temperature - provided each of those reported quantities is itself within the tolerance the calculation checks apply to it (peak demand and annual makeup within 10 percent of the recomputed values, supply temperature within the larger of 0.8 deg F and 10 percent of the approach). A reported quantity outside its tolerance is replaced by the recomputed value. The name is accepted when it is the smallest of the six margins so computed, with the same 0.004 tie. The roof area, structural and condenser flow margins depend only on published data and the schedule, so they are computed exactly.
P63: The design basis must also state which weather basis was applied and the clause that requires it, and which evaporation formulation was used.
P64: 9.1 Documented conflicts
P65: The project library contains documents that do not agree with one another. Paragraph 2 resolves several of those disagreements directly. The design basis must record how each of the three conflicts below was resolved, one line each, in the form below; these are the three this memorandum requires a line for, not a complete list of every place the library's documents differ:
P66:     CONFLICT <n>: ADOPTED <document> <clause> | SET ASIDE <document> <clause>
P67: where <document> is the designation the document gives itself and <clause> is the paragraph, table or revision within it. The three conflicts, in this order:
P68: A conflict is resolved by naming the document and clause that governs and the document and clause that does not. Both sides must be named. The grader reads these lines; it does not read prose around them.
P69: Appendix A - Deliverable formats
P70: A.1 CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf
P71: Plan units are feet, in the coordinates of M-401. Three layers are read:
P72:   M-CTWR-SCHD - one TEXT or MTEXT entity per scheduled field, written as '<TAG> <KEY> <VALUE>'. TAG is CT-1 ... CT-n for the cell rows and PLANT for the plant rows. Values are plain numbers or the listed keywords; units are not written into the value.
P73: MOTOREFF is the nominal full-load efficiency in percent. DRIFT is the drift rate in percent of design water flow. COC is the cycles of concentration the plant is controlled to. BASINCLR is the clear dimension in feet between the top of the roof and the underside of the tower basin. EVAPMETHOD is SATURATED-EXIT or LOSS-FACTOR. BASINHEATER, BLOWDOWNCTRL and EQUALIZING are YES or NO.
P74:   GPM is the flow through one cell with every installed cell in service, that is GPMTOTAL divided by CELLS. Where the staging rule of paragraph 6.6 leaves a cell out of service at some operating point, the scheduled figure does not change; the flow actually in each cell at each scenario belongs in the off-design table.
P75:   M-CTWR-PLAN - one closed LWPOLYLINE per cell, the rectangular plan outline of that cell's support frame, in the plan coordinates of M-401, which places the three plants on one sheet each on its own origin. One polyline per installed cell, no more and no fewer.
P76:   G-TBLK - the title block, including the sheet revision.
P77: A.2 CT_CALC_P.xlsx
P78: Five sheets. DesignPoint, WaterBalance, Energy and LifeCycleCost are two-column key/value sheets with the key in column A and the value in column B. OffDesign is a table with a header row.
P79: Values are numbers, not text with units, and no cell may be left blank or carry a placeholder.

P00: RFI-031 Response - Weather Basis, Redundancy Basis and Condenser Water Setpoint Policy
P01: Papago Federal Center | Response issued 21 August 2026 | Engineer of Record: Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
P02: Question 1
P03: The adopted HVAC criteria and the adopted agency facilities standard give different outdoor wet-bulb bases for evaporative machines. Which governs the tower selection, and which governs the failure-case calculation?
P04: Response 1
P05: Both govern, for different calculations, and neither is waived. Size the cells - the design point, the scheduled design approach and the redundancy capacity check - on the basis the HVAC criteria give for open cooling towers and wet closed-circuit cooling towers, which is the 1.0 percent annual wet-bulb temperature with the adder that clause states. Perform the cooling robustness (largest machine out of service) calculation on the evaporation design wet-bulb basis the agency facilities standard names in its cooling robustness requirement, with the same adder applied. Compute both percentiles from the station period of record identified in DC-02 paragraph 5.1. The cancelled engineering weather data criteria document in the project library is not a source of design values on this project.
P06: Question 2
P07: The agency standard requires variable frequency drives on the tower fans to control the condenser water supply temperature to the chillers, but does not state a reset policy. What policy should be scheduled?
P08: Response 2
P09: Schedule a wet-bulb-following reset with two numbers: a supply temperature floor and an offset above the outdoor wet-bulb temperature. The setpoint at any hour is the larger of the two, limited below by the minimum entering condenser water temperature of the chillers served. Both numbers are the designer's to optimise and both must appear on the tower schedule. A fixed setpoint is a special case with a zero offset and is not prohibited, but it is unlikely to be the least-energy policy at this site.
P10: Question 3
P11: The project library contains two industrial water treatment criteria documents with the same clause numbering, and two revisions of the roof mechanical plan. Which govern?
P12: Response 3
P13: The 2026 manual governs the water treatment criteria; the 2023 criteria document it replaced is retained for reference only. Revision C of M-401 governs the roof; Revision B is superseded and its equipment zone and outdoor air intake locations must not be used. Both supersessions are recorded in DC-02 paragraph 2.

FILE: /filesystem/final_batch4__mechanical_task3_ct_heat_lcc__blind/site/WT-01_Water_Treatment_Program_Memo.docx
P00: WT-01 Condenser Water Treatment Programme Memorandum
P01: Papago Federal Center | Revision 1, 14 August 2026 | Prepared by Verde Basin Water Technologies, Inc. for the Engineer of Record
P02: 1. Supply
P03: Condenser water makeup for all three plants is Class A+ reclaimed water delivered by the municipal purveyor from the reclamation facility, at the allocation and discharge limits of letter PW-LTR-014. The supply is the same for the three plants.
P04: 2. Analysis of record
P05: The analysis of record for the supply is the most recent COMPLETE analysis in the Water Quality Portal result set in the project library, where a complete analysis is one that reports dissolved calcium, dissolved alkalinity, total dissolved solids in mg/L, dissolved sulfate and dissolved silica from the same sampling date. Field-parameter-only visits are not complete analyses. Earlier complete analyses in the same result set are superseded by the most recent one and must not be used for the selection.
P06: Calcium is reported in the result set as mg/L as Ca. Calcium hardness as CaCO3 is the reported dissolved calcium multiplied by 2.497. The 'Hardness, Ca, Mg' result is total hardness and includes magnesium; it is not calcium hardness and must not be used in the indices. Where a determinand is reported both as dissolved and as recoverable, the dissolved result is used. Results reported in tons per acre-foot or tons per day are loading figures, not concentrations. Where total dissolved solids is reported in mg/L both as measured residue on evaporation and as a value computed from the constituents, the measured residue on evaporation is the value of record.
P07: 3. Programme
P08: The programme is a phosphonate and polymer stabilised alkaline programme with sulphuric acid feed. The acid feed holds the circulating M-alkalinity at 120 ppm as CaCO3 at all cycles of concentration; alkalinity therefore does not cycle up. Total dissolved solids and calcium hardness cycle up in proportion to the cycles of concentration. A conductivity controller with an automatic blowdown valve and metering pumps for the inhibitor and the biocide are required at every plant, as is a makeup water meter.
P09: 4. Controlling cycles of concentration
P10: The allowable cycles of concentration are the lowest of the limits the adopted water treatment manual gives for the scale-forming salts that this programme does not address, and the limit that the calcium carbonate scaling index of the same manual permits. The inhibitor package addresses calcium carbonate AND calcium sulfate, so neither the manual's rough calcium carbonate prediction nor its calcium sulfate prediction is a controlling limit here; calcium phosphate is not applicable because the circulating orthophosphate is held below 10 ppm by the programme. Silica is not addressed by the programme and its limit applies as the manual states it.
P11: The programme is qualified by the supplier to a computed Practical (Puckorius) Scaling Index of not less than 5.60. Below that value the dispersant cannot hold calcium carbonate in solution and the programme is not warranted. The index is evaluated at the hottest waterside temperature of the system, which for these plants is the condenser water return temperature at the design point - the return temperature the selected cells actually produce there (the CWR the calculation workbook's design point sheet reports), not a scheduled figure - and at the circulating concentrations that the selected cycles of concentration produce.
P12: 4.1 Evaluation of the index factors
P13: Factor B is taken from the manual's temperature table by linear interpolation. Factors A, C and D are the closed forms that the manual's tables tabulate, adopted here so that the index can be evaluated where the circulating concentration leaves the tabulated range:
P14:     A = (log10(total dissolved solids in ppm) - 1) / 10
P15:     C = log10(calcium hardness as CaCO3 in ppm) - 0.4
P16:     D = log10(M-alkalinity as CaCO3 in ppm)
P17: These reproduce the manual's tables across their whole tabulated range. The equilibrium pH is the closed form the manual's appendix gives as an alternative to its chart.
P18: 5. Other limits
P19: Circulating pH is controlled to 8.0 to 8.6. The blowdown discharged to the sanitary sewer must not exceed the daily limit of PW-LTR-014. Legionella control follows the campus water management plan and does not change the water balance.
P20: 6. Programme cost
P21: The programme is supplied as a full-service contract: inhibitor, dispersant, biocide, sulphuric acid, controller service and monthly testing, billed at $0.42 per 1,000 gallons of makeup water treated, at prices in effect on 1 October 2025. The contract price is adjusted for general inflation only.
================================================================================
FILE: /filesystem/final_batch4__mechanical_task3_ct_heat_lcc__blind/specs/23_25_00_HVAC_Water_Treatment_excerpt.docx
P00: SECTION 23 25 00 - HVAC WATER TREATMENT (EXCERPT)
P01: Papago Federal Center | Excerpt issued with the bid set for reference, 14 August 2026
P02: EXCERPT. This section covers the CLOSED hydronic systems of the project. The condenser water (open evaporative) treatment programme is specified in the water treatment memorandum WT-01 and is not covered by this section.
P03: 2.1 Closed loop chilled water and heating hot water
P04: Provide a nitrite-molybdate closed system inhibitor at 800 to 1,200 ppm as nitrite, with a tolyltriazole yellow metal inhibitor at 5 to 10 ppm. Maintain closed system pH between 8.5 and 10.5. Closed systems do not concentrate and have no cycles of concentration, no blowdown and no evaporative makeup.
P05: 2.2 Glycol
P06: Where freeze protection is required, use inhibited propylene glycol at 30 percent by volume, with a freeze point of -13 deg F and a burst point of -60 deg F. Ethylene glycol is prohibited. Correct the pump head and the heat transfer capacity for the glycol properties at the operating temperature: at 30 percent propylene glycol the specific heat is 0.90 and the specific gravity is 1.02 at 100 deg F, so the flow required for a given duty and range increases by approximately 9 percent.
P07: 2.3 Glycol feed
P08: Provide a 55 gallon glycol feed unit with a pressure switch, a low level alarm and a backflow preventer for each closed system requiring glycol.

P04: Factory assembled, induced draught, counterflow, film fill, field erected on structural steel dunnage, open evaporative cooling tower cells with variable frequency driven fans, for condenser water service.
P05: 1.2 Performance certification
P06: Thermal performance of each cell must be certified under CTI Standard STD-201 for the scheduled duty. Where a model is not certified, a field acceptance test under CTI ATC-105 at the contractor's expense is required.
P07: PART 2 - PRODUCTS
P08: 2.1 Acceptable manufacturers
P09: Cells of the CTX Series C range in submittal VD-01, or an approved equal of the same certified capability, plan dimensions and operating weight.
P10: 2.2 Materials
P11: Water contact surfaces, including the cold water basin, the casing below the operating water line, the distribution basin and all fasteners in the water stream, must comply with the materials requirement of the agency facilities standard for cooling towers. Confirm the selected material option against that requirement; the manufacturer offers options that do not comply. Structural steel dunnage is hot-dip galvanised after fabrication; dunnage is not a water contact surface.
P12: 2.3 Drift eliminators
P13: Cellular PVC drift eliminators, removable in sections. The certified drift rate of the selected eliminator must not exceed 0.002 percent of the design circulating water flow rate at design air flow. Eliminator classes and their certified drift rates are in submittal VD-04. The drift rate used in the water balance must be the certified rate of the eliminator actually selected.
P14: 2.4 Basin and blowdown
P15: Cold water basin with a sloped sump, sweeper piping, an overflow, a drain, a make-up connection with an electrically actuated valve and an air gap, and an electrically actuated automatic blowdown valve controlled from a conductivity controller. Provide connections and mounting for the chemical metering pumps of the water treatment programme. A basin heater and heat traced make-up piping are provided only where the design criteria memorandum requires them.
P16: 2.5 Fans and drives
P17: Axial propeller fans on right angle gear reducers, with a variable frequency drive on each fan motor. Fan motors are totally enclosed fan cooled, squirrel cage induction, NEMA Design B, suitable for inverter duty, and must comply with the federal energy conservation standard for the applicable motor category. The fan must not draw more than the motor nameplate horsepower at any operating point in the scheduled sequence; the gear reducer service factor is not available as fan power.
P18: 2.6 Sound
P19: The A-weighted sound power level of each cell at full fan speed must not exceed 102 dB re 1 pW. Sound power levels of the offered cells are in submittal VD-01.
P20: 2.7 Equalising and isolation
P21: Where more than one cell is installed, provide equalising lines between the cold water basins and automatic isolation valves on the supply to each cell, so that any cell may be taken out of service with its chiller running, as the agency facilities standard requires.
P22: PART 3 - EXECUTION
P23: 3.1 Installation
P24: Set cells on structural steel dunnage on the roof framing zones indicated on S-401, within the equipment zone indicated on M-401 Revision C. Maintain the air inlet clearances of submittal VD-01 on every air inlet face and between adjacent cells, and the clearance between the top of the roof and the underside of the basin that the agency facilities standard requires.

P00: EC-01 Life-Cycle Cost Analysis Criteria - Condenser Water Heat Rejection Replacement
P01: Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 0, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC for the General Services Administration
P02: 1. Governing rule
P03: The tower selection for each plant is an energy and water conservation investment in a Federal building and is selected under the Federal life-cycle cost methodology of 10 CFR Part 436, Subpart A (copy in standards/). The alternative tower selections for a plant are mutually exclusive alternatives for one building energy system. Each plant is designed for the HIGHEST NET SAVINGS, in the sense of 10 CFR 436.18(e) and 436.20, relative to the basic design of paragraph 5, among the designs that meet every requirement of the adopted criteria and of DC-02. Net savings of a design = life-cycle cost of the basic design - life-cycle cost of the design.
P04: 2. Base date and analysis basis
P05: The base date of the analysis is 1 October 2025, the first day of the FY2026 base year. The analysis is a constant-dollar analysis at base-date prices with the real discount rate (10 CFR 436.14(a)), using the end-of-year conventions of the tables it takes its factors from.
P06: 3. Schedule
P07: The design and construction period is 1 year from the base date; beneficial occupancy of the replaced plants is 1 October 2026. Investment costs are taken as a lump sum at the base date (10 CFR 436.14(f)). Energy, water and operation and maintenance costs begin to accrue at beneficial occupancy, not at the base date (436.14(g)); their present values are found as 10 CFR 436.16(c), 436.17(b) and 436.17(d) direct for costs that begin to accrue after the base date.
P08: 4. Discount rate, energy escalation and present-value factors
P09: The discount rate, the projected escalation of energy prices and the present-value factors are those of the Annual Supplement to NIST Handbook 135 in force at the base date, as 10 CFR 436.14(a) and (b) require: the 2025 edition. Its data tables - NIST data release doi:10.18434/mds2-3848 - are in economics/ and govern every rate and factor. The project library holds the text of the 2024 edition (NIST IR 85-3273-39) for its explanation of the tables and the method; the tables and the method are organised the same way in both editions, but every rate, factor and worked-example number printed in the 2024 edition is SUPERSEDED by the 2025 data release and must not be used.
P10: Energy conservation projects use the DOE (FEMP) factors and discount rate, not the OMB Circular A-94 factors, which apply to other Federal investments. The site is in Arizona; the electricity is purchased under the commercial general service schedule of letter UT-01. Take the factors for that location, that sector and that fuel. Use the tables as they are printed, without shifting their base year: the year counts of the tables are years from the base date of this analysis.
P11: 5. Basic design
P12: The basic design of 10 CFR 436.20 for each plant is the replacement of the existing cells in kind, operated as the existing plants are operated:
P13: The basic design is evaluated with the same simulation basis, scenario bins, staging and control conventions as a proposed design (DC-02) and priced exactly as a proposed design is priced (paragraph 6). It is a reference for net savings only; it is not required to meet the criteria and it is not a candidate selection.
P14: 6. Cost data
P15: The water quantities priced in the analysis are those of the SATURATED-EXIT formulation of DC-02 paragraph 7 - the adopted simulation basis - for the proposed design and the basic design alike, whichever formulation the water balance of the calculation workbook is reported in. The allocation and discharge limits of PW-LTR-014 are checked in the formulation the workbook declares.
P16: 7. Study period, replacement and salvage
P17: The study period is set by 10 CFR 436.14(d)(2)(i) for mutually exclusive alternatives, the alternatives being the tower selections VD-01 and VD-05 offer that the adopted criteria admit, with their design service lives from the VD-05 ServiceLife sheet. The study period runs from the base date: the design and construction period of paragraph 3 followed by the service period. A cell placed in service at beneficial occupancy with a service life shorter than the service period is replaced when its life expires, at the installed price of one cell as VD-05 states it; the plant controls item is not replaced. Salvage value at the end of the study period is straight-line: the replacement cost multiplied by the unexpired fraction of the service life of the equipment then in service. Replacement and salvage are single amounts discounted from the year in which they occur.
P18: 8. Reporting
P19: Each plant's calculation workbook carries the LifeCycleCost sheet of DC-02 Appendix A.2 with the parameters and results of this analysis for the design as scheduled.

escalation rate must also be expressed in real terms. If the discount rate is expressed in nominal

In Tables A-1, A-2, and A-3 (a,b,c) SPV, UPV, and UPV* factors are provided for both the DOE 
and the OMB Circular A-94 real discount rates current as of the date of this publication. The 
FEMP SPV, UPV, and UPV* factors were computed using the DOE discount rate. The FEMP 
factors are for finding the present value of future costs associated with federal energy and 
water conservation projects and renewable energy projects. The OMB SPV, UPV, and UPV* 
factors were computed using the OMB discount rates. The OMB factors are for finding the 
present value of future costs associated with most other federal projects (except those 
specifically exempted from OMB Circular A-94). The DOE and OMB discount rates used in 
computing these tables are real rates, exclusive of general price inflation. Thus, the resulting 
discount factors are intended for use with future costs that are stated in constant dollars. 
Note: We have added to table A-3a a column of UPV* factors that incorporate an escalation 
rate of -1.2 %, the negative of the inflation rate used to calculate the DOE nominal discount rate 
for 2024. The UPV* factors in this column can be used to calculate present values of fixed dollar 
amounts when performing a constant-dollar analysis. An example might be a fixed contract 
payment in an ESPC project. For these fixed amounts, the assumption that in a constant-dollar 
analysis all cash flows change at the rate of general inflation (so that the differential escalation 
rate is zero) does not apply. In real terms, fixed amounts change at a differential rate equal to 
the negative of the inflation rate.  
Examples of How to Use the Factors: 
 
SPV (FEMP): To compute the present value of a replacement cost expected to occur in the 8th 
year for an energy efficient heating system, go to Table A-1, find the 3.0 % SPV factor for year 8 
(0.789), and multiply the factor by the replacement cost as of the base date. 
SPV (OMB, Short-term): To compute the present value of a repair cost in the 5th year for a floor 
covering (non-energy related), go to Table A-1, find the 1.4 % SPV factor for year 5 (0.933), and 
multiply the factor by the repair cost as of the base date. 
SPV (OMB, Long-term): To compute the present value of a repair cost in the 15th year for a 
floor covering (non-energy related), go to Table A-1, find the 2.0 % SPV factor for year 15 
(0.743), and multiply the factor by the repair cost as of the base date. 
UPV (FEMP): To compute the present value of an annually recurring maintenance cost for a 
renewable energy system over 20 years, go to Table A-2, find the 3.0 % UPV factor for 20 years 
(14.877), and multiply the factor by the annual maintenance cost as of the base date. 
UPV (OMB, Short-term): To compute the present value of annually recurring costs of office 
cleaning over 10 years (for a project not primarily related to energy conservation), go to Table 
A-2, find the 1.4 % UPV factor for 10 years (9.271), and multiply the factor by the annual 
cleaning cost as of the base date.

UPV (OMB, Long-term): To compute the present value of annually recurring costs of office 
cleaning over 25 years (for a project not primarily related to energy conservation), go to Table 
A-2, find the 2.0 % UPV factor for 25 years (19.523), and multiply the factor by the annual 
cleaning cost as of the base date. 
UPV* (all): To compute the present value of annually recurring costs of water usage which are 
expected to increase at 2.0 % faster than the rate of general inflation over 25 years, find the 
UPV* factor from table A-3 (a, b, or c as appropriate) that corresponds to 2% escalation and a 
25-year study period. From table A-3a (3.0 % DOE discount rate) the corresponding UPV* factor 
is 22.08. Multiply this factor by the annual water cost as computed at base year prices to 
determine the present value of these water costs over the entire 25 years. 
UPV* (negative inflation rate): To compute the present value of an annually recurring contract 
payment that is fixed over a contract period of 10 years, find the UPV* factor from table A-3a 
that corresponds to an escalation of 1.0 % and a 10-year time period. From table A-3a (3.0 % 
DOE discount rate) the corresponding UPV* factor is 8.99. Multiply this factor by the annual 
contract payment as of the base year to determine the present value of these contract 
payments over the entire 10-year period. 
Note: UPV factors are generally applied to costs that recur annually in substantially the same 
amount. Examples of such costs are routine operating and maintenance costs. UPV* factors are 
generally applied to costs that recur annually but change from year to year at a constant 
escalation rate. Examples of such costs are water usage costs when they increase from year to 
year. These costs usually occur every year over the service period of the building life. If there is a 
planning/design/construction period before the service life begins, during which these annual 
costs are not incurred, the appropriate UPV (or UPV*) factor for the service period is the 
difference between the UPV (or UPV*) factor for the entire study period and the UPV (or UPV*) 
factor for the planning/design/construction period. For example, if the planning/ 
design/construction period is 3 years and the service period is 25 years, for a total study period 
of 28 years, the corresponding UPV factor (from Table A-2, DOE 3.0 % discount rate) is 18.764 – 
2.829 =15.935.  
For further explanation and illustration of how to use these factors, see NIST Handbook 135. 
 Modified Uniform Present Value Factors for Fuel Costs 
This section presents FEMP and OMB modified uniform present value (UPV*) discount factors 
for calculating the present value of energy usage for federal projects. Factors are provided for 
the four major Census regions and for the overall United States. The factors are modified in the 
sense that they incorporate energy price escalation rates based on future energy prices 
projected by DOE for the years 2024 to 2054. There are two sets of UPV* tables: the "Ba" tables 
present FEMP UPV* factors based on the DOE discount rate (3.0 % real), and the "Bb" tables 
present OMB UPV* factors based on two OMB discount rates (1.4 % real for short-term study 
periods of 1 to 10 years, 2.0 % real for long-term study periods of 11 to 30 years). The 
underlying energy price indices for the years 2024 to 2054, on which these UPV* calculations 
are based, are shown in tables Ca-1 through Ca-5. The corresponding average energy price

through Cb-5. 
Energy Price Projections. The FEMP and OMB UPV* factors incorporate energy price escalation 
rates computed from future energy prices projected by the EIA. Energy prices through 2050 
were generated by EIA using the National Energy Modeling System (NEMS) and published in the 
AEO2023 [3]. Note that AEO 2023 has been used because no AEO is being released in 2024. The 
projection period for the AEO2023 projections is through 2050«ForecastYearEnd». Any years 
beyond the EIA projections are extrapolated assuming escalation equivalent to the simple 
average of the last 5 years of EIA projections (2046 through 2050). 
NEMS is an energy market model designed to project the impacts of alternative energy policies 
or assumptions on U.S. energy markets. NEMS produces projections of the U.S. energy future, 
given current laws and policies and other key assumptions, including macroeconomic indicators 
from Data Resources, Inc., the production policy of the Organization of Petroleum Exporting 
Countries, the size of the economically recoverable resource base for fossil fuels, and the rate 
of development and penetration of new technologies. NEMS balances energy supply and 
demands with modules representing primary fuel supply, end-use demand for four sectors, and 
conversion of energy by refineries and electricity generators. Macroeconomic and international 
oil modules reflect the impacts of energy prices, production, and consumption on world oil 
markets and the economy. 
The EIA energy price projections presented in this report, like those of other forecasts, are 
dependent on the data, methodologies, and specific assumptions used in their development. 
Many of the assumptions concerning the future cannot be known with any degree of certainty. 
Thus, the projections are not statements of what will happen, but what might happen given the 
specific assumptions and methodologies used. Although EIA has endeavored to make these 
forecasts as objective, reliable, and useful as possible, these projections should serve as an 
adjunct to, not a substitute for, the analytical process. The AEO2023 was prepared by EIA as 
required under statute by federal legislation. The price projections to 2050 were prepared in 
accordance with a Service Request from the Federal Energy Management Program. 
Note: Section 441 of the Energy Independence and Security Act of 2007 (EISA) extends from 25 
years to 40 years the maximum service period for conducting FEMP life-cycle cost analyses. To 
account for the legislated change, the BLCC program now incorporates unofficial projections of 
future energy prices beyond 2050 to accommodate FEMP service periods of up to 40 years. The 
projections are based on simple average growth rate of the last 5 years of EIA projections. BLCC 
users should exercise caution when interpreting energy cost savings beyond 30 years and do 
sensitivity analyses to test different out-year assumptions.

2.2.1. FEMP Modified Uniform Present Value Factors 
The FEMP Modified Uniform Present Value (FEMP UPV*) factors presented in the "Ba" tables, 
based on the current DOE discount rate (3.0 %), are for calculating the present value of energy 
costs or savings accruing over 1 year to 30 years and are to be used in life-cycle cost analyses of 
federal energy conservation and renewable energy projects. These factors may be applied to 
projects with or without planning/design/construction periods, as shown below. 
These factors apply only to annual energy usage or energy savings that are assumed to be the 
same each year over the service period. The BLCC computer program can compute the present 
value of energy usage and savings that are not the same in each year. 
Examples of How to Use the FEMP UPV* Factors: 
FEMP UPV*, no planning/design/construction period: To compute the present value of heating 
with natural gas over 25 years in a federal office building in New Mexico, go to Table Ba-4, find 
the FEMP UPV* factor for commercial natural gas for 25 years (17.07), and multiply this factor 
by the annual heating cost at base-date natural gas prices. 
FEMP UPV*, with planning/design/construction period: To compute a present value factor for a 
service period following a planning/design/construction period (1) find the FEMP UPV* factor 
for the combined length of the planning/design/construction period and the service period, and 
(2) subtract from (1) the FEMP UPV* factor for the planning/design/ construction period alone. 
The difference is the FEMP UPV* factor for the years over which energy costs or savings accrue.

energy conserving design options. It is expected to have a planning/design/construction period 
of 5 years, after which it will be occupied for 25 years. To compute the present value of natural 
gas costs over 25 years of occupancy, go to Table Ba-1 and find the FEMP UPV* factors for 
commercial natural gas for 5 years (4.02) and for 30 years (16.82). The difference (12.80) is the 
FEMP UPV* factor for natural gas costs over 25 years, beginning 5 years after the base date. 
Multiply 12.80 by the annual natural gas cost at base date prices (not occupancy-date prices) to 
calculate the present value of natural gas costs over the entire 25-year occupancy period. 
2.2.2. OMB Modified Uniform Present Value Factors 
The OMB Modified Uniform Present Value (OMB UPV*) factors presented in the "Bb" tables, 
based on the current OMB discount rates (1.4 % short term and 2.0 % long term), are for 
calculating the present value of energy costs accruing over 1 year to 30 years when conducting 
a life-cycle cost analysis of a federal project not explicitly related to energy or water 
conservation or renewable resources. These factors apply only to annual energy usage that is 
assumed to be the same each year over the service period. The BLCC computer program can 
compute the present value of energy usage and savings that are not the same in each year. 
Examples of How to Use the OMB UPV* Factors: 
OMB UPV* (OMB discount rate): To compute the present value over 30 years of electricity costs 
associated with the occupancy of a federal office building in Ohio (where energy conservation is 
not a specific consideration in the LCC analysis), go to Table Bb-2, find the OMB UPV* factor for 
commercial electricity for 30 years (20.32), and multiply this factor by the annual electricity cost 
in base-date dollars.
