P25: Each chiller has a dedicated constant-speed condenser water pump. The scheduled design flow is the flow with every chiller running; the flow with n chillers running is n/N of it. The per-chiller flow must lie inside the condenser flow limits of submittal VD-03 and the per-cell flow inside the limits of submittal VD-01.
P26: 6.3 Redundancy
P27: The plant must meet its design block load with the largest single cell out of service, at the failure-case wet-bulb basis of paragraph 5.2, with the remaining cells at full fan speed, and at an entering condenser water temperature no warmer than the machines' published maximum (submittal VD-03). This is the cooling robustness performance tier the agency facilities standard requires.
P28: With a cell out of service the design condenser water flow is unchanged - every chiller is still running on its dedicated constant-speed pump (paragraph 6.2) - and it is carried by the cells that remain in service. The flow through each remaining cell in that state must lie inside the per-cell flow limits of submittal VD-01 and inside the water flow rate ratio limits of the performance object (paragraph 6.8). A plant whose remaining cells would have to pass more than that does not meet this requirement, whatever temperature a calculation extrapolated beyond those limits might predict: a cell above its rated distribution capacity and outside the validity envelope of its performance model has no substantiated capability. The clamping described in the second part of paragraph 6.8 applies to the inlet wet-bulb temperature only; it does not apply to the water flow rate ratio, in this case or any other.
P29: 6.4 Condenser water pump power
P30: Condenser water pump total head is taken as a fixed static lift plus a friction component that varies with the square of the flow ratio:
P31: H = H_static + (H_pipe + H_condenser) x (Q / Q_ref)^2        [ft of water]
P32: Pump shaft power = Q x H / (3960 x eta_pump)                 [hp, Q in gpm]
P33: Pump electrical input = shaft power x 0.7457 / eta_motor     [kW]
P34: where Q is the flow through one pump. The per-plant constants are:
P35: 6.5 Chiller staging
P36: Chillers stage on in order: the smallest number of machines whose available capacity at the operating leaving chilled water and entering condenser water temperatures meets the block load runs, and the load is divided equally between them.
P37: Available capacity here is the capacity the adopted performance data set makes available at those temperatures: the machine's reference capacity multiplied by its capacity-as-a-function-of-temperature curve evaluated at the operating point, and nothing else. The maximum part load ratio is not part of available capacity. It is a separate published limit - the ceiling on the load a machine that is already running may be given - and it is not applied to the capacity that decides how many machines run.
P38: 6.6 Cell staging
P39: Condenser water is distributed to every installed cell unless the resulting per-cell flow would fall below the effective minimum, which is the larger of the submittal's minimum per-cell flow and the flow at which the performance object's minimum water flow rate ratio is reached. Cells are then isolated one at a time until the per-cell flow is at or above the effective minimum. Tower fans of the cells in service modulate together.
P40: 6.7 Condenser water supply temperature control
P41: The condenser water supply temperature setpoint is scheduled as a wet-bulb-following reset: the setpoint is the larger of a scheduled floor and the outdoor wet-bulb temperature plus a scheduled offset, and is in no case below the minimum entering condenser water temperature the chillers are rated for. The fans modulate to the setpoint exactly as the reference implementation models a variable speed tower: full speed when the setpoint cannot be met, free convection when the fans are not needed, minimum speed with cycling below that. A condenser water bypass valve holds the setpoint when the tower would otherwise overcool, so the supply temperature never falls below the setpoint.
P42: 6.8 Validity of the performance correlation
P43: A cell may not be operated at a water flow rate ratio outside the limits stated in the performance object, because the implementation clamps the ratio there and the capability would not be substantiated. The range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits of the same object apply at every scenario. A design that operates outside them is not accepted.
P44: The inlet air wet-bulb temperature is treated differently, and deliberately. The reference implementation clamps it to the object's stated range before evaluating the correlation, so an outdoor wet bulb at or above the object's maximum is evaluated AT that maximum and is never extrapolated. The design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 lands on that maximum at this site. That is not an error and no work-around is required: it is what the adopted simulation basis does, and the wet-bulb limit is therefore not one of the envelope limits this paragraph tests.
P45: 6.9 Design point
P46: At the design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 and the design block load, with every chiller running at the scheduled design flow and the cells in service at full fan speed, the cells must deliver condenser water no warmer than the scheduled design supply temperature (CWSDESIGN), and the chillers must carry the design block load at that entering condenser water temperature. The validity limits of paragraph 6.8 - the water flow rate ratio limits, and the range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits - apply at this design point as they do at every scenario. A schedule may be conservative: a CWSDESIGN warmer than the selected cells actually need is acceptable.
P47: 6.10 Peak coincident demand
P48: The peak coincident electrical demand of a plant is the largest total electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps operating together, taken over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 and over nothing else. It is a maximum over those bins, not a design-day figure: neither the design point of paragraph 6.9 nor the redundancy case of paragraph 6.3 is a scenario bin - they are sizing conditions - and neither enters this maximum. Basin heaters, controls and lighting are not part of it. This is the quantity the motor control centre's spare capacity limits and the quantity the calculation workbook reports.
P49: 7. Water
P50: The water balance, the cycles of concentration and the treatment programme are governed by the adopted water treatment manual and by the reclaimed water correspondence and treatment memorandum in the project library.
P51: Two evaporation formulations are adopted for this project, and they are these two, named so that the choice is between two fully specified methods:
P52: SATURATED-EXIT - the moist-air method of the reference implementation's tower water-use routine: the outlet air is saturated at the inlet enthalpy plus the water-side heat transfer divided by the air mass flow, and the evaporated mass is the air mass flow times the rise in specific humidity, converted to a volume with the density of water. As the routine computes them, the inlet enthalpy is that of saturated air at the inlet wet-bulb temperature, and the water density is taken at the mean of the inlet dry-bulb and the saturated outlet air temperatures, not below 4 deg C. The routine reads that density from fluid property tables that are not part of the shipped source; on this project it is taken as rho = 1000 x (1 - (T + 288.9414) / (508929.2 x (T + 68.12963)) x (T - 3.9863)^2) kg/m3, T in deg C. Every other quantity the method needs is in the shipped source and its header.
P53: LOSS-FACTOR - the rule of thumb of the adopted water treatment manual's cooling tower chapter, with the constant and the temperature basis that chapter states and its own worked example confirms. It is NOT the reference implementation's user-factor path: that path reads a loss factor from an input field this project does not set, and the input dictionary that would supply a default for it is not part of the adopted basis.
P54: Either may be used. The design basis must state which one was used, and the water balance of the submitted workbook must be computed consistently with the stated choice throughout.
P55: 8. Deliverable
P56: For each plant P in {CUP, ANNEX, LAB} deliver CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf and CT_CALC_P.xlsx, and once for the package constraint_register.csv and design_basis.md. Appendix A fixes the formats.
P57: 9. Design basis content
P58: The design basis must state, for each plant, the governing constraint on the design in the form:
P59: GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <plant>: <name> (relative margin <value>)
P60: where <name> is exactly one of the following six, and is the one with the smallest relative margin at the submitted design, and <value> is that relative margin:
P61: The six names above are the only admissible values of <name>. Where two of them are within 0.004 of each other at the submitted design, either may be stated.
P62: The margins are judged against the quantities the calculation workbook reports, not against a figure to a precision the workbook cannot carry. A relative margin is a small difference divided by a limit, so it is far more sensitive than the quantity it is computed from: near a limit, a 1 percent difference in peak demand can move the margin by more than half its value. The stated margin is therefore accepted when it agrees, within 0.004, with the margin computed from the workbook's own reported peak coincident demand, annual makeup and design supply temperature - provided each of those reported quantities is itself within the tolerance the calculation checks apply to it (peak demand and annual makeup within 10 percent of the recomputed values, supply temperature within the larger of 0.8 deg F and 10 percent of the approach). A reported quantity outside its tolerance is replaced by the recomputed value. The name is accepted when it is the smallest of the six margins so computed, with the same 0.004 tie. The roof area, structural and condenser flow margins depend only on published data and the schedule, so they are computed exactly.
P63: The design basis must also state which weather basis was applied and the clause that requires it, and which evaporation formulation was used.
P64: 9.1 Documented conflicts
P65: The project library contains documents that do not agree with one another. Paragraph 2 resolves several of those disagreements directly. The design basis must record how each of the three conflicts below was resolved, one line each, in the form below; these are the three this memorandum requires a line for, not a complete list of every place the library's documents differ:
P66: CONFLICT <n>: ADOPTED <document> <clause> | SET ASIDE <document> <clause>
P67: where <document> is the designation the document gives itself and <clause> is the paragraph, table or revision within it. The three conflicts, in this order:
P68: A conflict is resolved by naming the document and clause that governs and the document and clause that does not. Both sides must be named. The grader reads these lines; it does not read prose around them.
P69: Appendix A - Deliverable formats
P70: A.1 CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf
P71: Plan units are feet, in the coordinates of M-401. Three layers are read:
P72: M-CTWR-SCHD - one TEXT or MTEXT entity per scheduled field, written as '<TAG> <KEY> <VALUE>'. TAG is CT-1 ... CT-n for the cell rows and PLANT for the plant rows. Values are plain numbers or the listed keywords; units are not written into the value.
P73: MOTOREFF is the nominal full-load efficiency in percent. DRIFT is the drift rate in percent of design water flow. COC is the cycles of concentration the plant is controlled to. BASINCLR is the clear dimension in feet between the top of the roof and the underside of the tower basin. EVAPMETHOD is SATURATED-EXIT or LOSS-FACTOR. BASINHEATER, BLOWDOWNCTRL and EQUALIZING are YES or NO.
P74: GPM is the flow through one cell with every installed cell in service, that is GPMTOTAL divided by CELLS. Where the staging rule of paragraph 6.6 leaves a cell out of service at some operating point, the scheduled figure does not change; the flow actually in each cell at each scenario belongs in the off-design table.
P75: M-CTWR-PLAN - one closed LWPOLYLINE per cell, the rectangular plan outline of that cell's support frame, in the plan coordinates of M-401, which places the three plants on one sheet each on its own origin. One polyline per installed cell, no more and no fewer.
P76: G-TBLK - the title block, including the sheet revision.
P77: A.2 CT_CALC_P.xlsx
P78: Five sheets. DesignPoint, WaterBalance, Energy and LifeCycleCost are two-column key/value sheets with the key in column A and the value in column B. OffDesign is a table with a header row.
P79: Values are numbers, not text with units, and no cell may be left blank or carry a placeholder.
P80: RedundancyCapacity_tons is the total cooling capacity the plant's chillers can deliver with the largest tower cell out of service, evaluated at the failure-case wet bulb of paragraph 6.3 with the remaining cells at full fan speed, at the entering condenser water temperature those remaining cells actually produce at that wet bulb and at the scheduled condenser water flow. It is the capacity available at that operating point, not the capacity available at the machine's rated maximum entering condenser water temperature, and not the reference capacity of the performance data set. It is available capacity in the sense of paragraph 6.5, so the maximum part load ratio is not applied to it. RedundancyWetBulb_F is the wet bulb it is evaluated at.
P81: LifeCycleCost: DiscountRate is the real discount rate as a fraction or in percent. StudyPeriod_yr and ConstructionPeriod_yr are in years from the base date. UPVStarElectricity, UPVStarWater and UPVNonFuel are the present-value factors the analysis multiplies the base-year annual electricity cost, water and sewer cost, and non-fuel operation and maintenance cost by, to give their present values at the base date over the period in which they accrue. AnnualEnergyCost_USD (energy and demand charges), AnnualWaterCost_USD (reclaimed water and sewer) and AnnualOMCost_USD (treatment and routine maintenance) are base-year amounts; PVEnergy_USD, PVWater_USD and PVOM_USD their present values; PVReplacement_USD and PVSalvage_USD the present values of replacements and of the salvage value (a positive number, subtracted in LCC_USD); LCC_USD the life-cycle cost of the design as scheduled, BasicDesignLCC_USD that of the EC-01 basic design of the same plant, and NetSavings_USD their difference. All dollar amounts are constant base-date dollars.
P82: FanPLR is the fan part load ratio of the cells in service at that scenario bin, as the reference implementation of paragraph 6.7 reports it for a variable speed tower: 1.0 where the fans run, whether at full speed or modulating to the setpoint; 0.0 where the fans are off; and the cycling ratio where the cells cycle at the minimum fan speed. The speed itself is reported separately as AirFlowRatio.
P83: The DesignPoint sheet reports the performance the SELECTED equipment achieves at the design point - the range, approach, supply and return temperatures and water flow rate ratio that follow from the scheduled model, cell count and flow - and not the scheduled target. Where a design is scheduled conservatively, so that CWSDESIGN is warmer than the cells actually need, the schedule carries the conservative number and this sheet carries the achieved one.

P00: DC-02 Mechanical Design Criteria Memorandum - Condenser Water Heat Rejection
P01: Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 3, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
This memorandum supersedes DC-02 Revision 2 in its entirety. Revision 3 adds the life-cycle cost objective (paragraph 4, EC-01) and the LifeCycleCost sheet of Appendix A.2.
P02: 1. Scope
P03: This memorandum states the criteria, conventions and deliverable requirements for the replacement of the condenser water heat rejection plants serving the Courthouse Central Utility Plant (CUP), the Data Annex (ANNEX) and the Laboratory Wing (LAB). The chillers, the condenser water pumps' hydraulic circuits and the electrical distribution are existing or already procured and are not in the scope of this design.
P04: 2. Adopted criteria
P05: 3. Plants and served loads
P06: Block cooling loads as a function of outdoor dry-bulb temperature are scheduled on M-603. Chiller performance data and condenser water limits are on M-601 and submittal VD-03.
P07: 4. Objective
P08: Each plant must be designed for the HIGHEST LIFE-CYCLE NET SAVINGS, relative to the basic design, consistent with every requirement of the adopted criteria and of this memorandum, with the life-cycle cost analysis performed as EC-01 directs under 10 CFR Part 436 Subpart A. It is not the design with the lowest energy, nor the one with the lowest first cost, unless the analysis makes it so.
P09: Annual plant electrical energy - the energy quantity the analysis prices - is the sum over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 of the bin hours multiplied by the coincident electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps of that plant.
P10: 5. Climatic and property basis
P11: 5.1 Governing station
P12: The climatic basis is the National Centers for Environmental Information Local Climatological Data record of the airport station serving the site, for the three complete calendar years in the project library. That record is the period of record (POR) for every percentile in this memorandum. Only observations whose report type is FM-15 or FM-16 are counted; the daily and monthly summary rows of the record are not observations. Records for any other station in the library are not part of the POR.
P13: 5.2 Design outdoor conditions
P14: A percentile design value is the value that was exceeded that percentage of the observations over the entire POR, taken as a single annual population (not a seasonal one). The design outdoor wet-bulb temperature for the heat rejection equipment is the 1.0 percent annual wet-bulb temperature so computed, adjusted as the adopted HVAC criteria require for open cooling towers. The failure-case calculation of paragraph 6.3 uses the wet-bulb basis that the adopted agency facilities standard prescribes for evaporative machines, adjusted the same way. Do not take design values from the cancelled weather-data criteria document.
P15: 5.3 Scenario bins
P16: Annual performance is evaluated on scenario bins formed from the POR observations: bin each observation by wet-bulb temperature in 2 deg F bins and by dry-bulb temperature in 5 deg F bins, take the bin condition as the bin mid-points, and scale the bin counts so that the bins total 8760 hours per year. The block load of a bin is the M-603 load at the bin dry-bulb temperature. Where a bin's dry-bulb mid-point would fall below its wet-bulb mid-point, the dry-bulb temperature is taken equal to the wet-bulb mid-point. The bin edges fall at whole multiples of the bin width measured from zero deg F: an observation belongs to the bin whose lower edge is the largest such multiple that does not exceed it, the lower edge belonging to the bin and the upper edge to the next one, so that a bin's mid-point is its lower edge plus half the bin width.
P17: 5.4 Freeze protection
P18: A basin heater and heat-traced makeup piping are required only where the 99.6 percent annual dry-bulb temperature computed from the POR is at or below 32 deg F. The design basis must state the computed 99.6 percent dry-bulb temperature and the determination that follows from it.
P19: 5.5 Property basis
P20: Moist air properties are those of the psychrometric routines of the reference implementation in the project library (saturation pressure over water, humidity ratio from dry- and wet-bulb, moist air enthalpy and density, and saturation temperature from enthalpy). The barometric pressure is the mean station pressure of the governing POR, not a sea-level or a standard-atmosphere value. Water is taken at 8.33 lb/gal and 1.0 BTU/lb-deg F, so that heat rejection in BTU/h is 500 times the flow in gpm times the range in deg F.
P21: 6. Plant configuration and operating conventions
P22: 6.1 Cells and controls
P23: All cells of a plant are of one model and one size and carry identical fan, motor, drift eliminator and material selections. Every tower fan motor is driven by a variable frequency drive. The number of cells must be a whole multiple of the number of chillers served.
P24: 6.2 Condenser water flow

CHAPTER 1 INTRODUCTION 
1-1 
BACKGROUND. 
Clearly defining water treatment requirements for industrial water continue to be critical 
to reduce maintenance cost and increase life expectancy on all equipment. 
1-2 
REISSUES AND CANCELS. 
This UFM supersedes UFC-3-230-13, Industrial Water Treatment Operation and 
Maintenance, 1 March 2023. 
1-3 
PURPOSE AND SCOPE. 
This UFM provides an overview of industrial water treatment operations and 
maintenance.  As used in this UFM, the term “industrial water” refers to the water used 
in power generation, heating, air conditioning, refrigeration, cooling, processing and all 
other equipment and systems that require water for operation.  This UFM covers Theory 
of Operation, cause and effect, prevention, and it provides specific performance criteria 
and minimally acceptable standards for water treatment programs as a whole. 
1-4 
APPLICABILITY. 
This UFM applies to industrial water systems.  Industrial water is not the same as 
potable water. Industrial water is never consumed or used under situations that require 
a high degree of sanitation.  To provide DOD personnel with the most up-to-date 
information available, the UFM guides the reader to industry standards in the industrial 
water treatment of heating, cooling and ship to shore equipment. 
1-5 
GENERAL BUILDING REQUIREMENTS. 
Comply with UFC 1-200-01, DoD Building Code. UFC 1-200-01 provides applicability of 
model building codes and government unique criteria for typical design disciplines and 
building systems, as well as for accessibility, antiterrorism, security, high performance 
and sustainability requirements, and safety.  Use this UFM in addition to UFC 1-200-01 
and the UFCs and government criteria referenced therein. 
1-6 
CYBERSECURITY. 
All control systems (including systems separate from an energy management control 
system) must be planned, designed, acquired, executed, and maintained in accordance 
with UFC 4-010-06, and as required by individual Service Implementation Policy. 
1-7 
GLOSSARY. 
Appendix F contains acronyms, abbreviations, and terms.

P00: UT-01 Electric Service - Rate Confirmation
P01: Papago Electric Service Company | 22 September 2025 | to the General Services Administration, Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona
P02: This letter confirms the rate schedule under which the Papago Federal Center campus takes electric service, for use in the life-cycle cost analysis of the condenser water heat rejection replacement. The campus is served at 12.47 kV through a single campus meter.
P03: 1. Applicable schedule
P04: Rate Schedule GS-L, General Service - Large (commercial). The campus is a non-residential, non-industrial customer and is billed under the commercial general service schedules of the Company.
P05: 2. Billing demand
P06: The billing demand for a month is the greater of (a) the highest 15-minute demand measured in that month and (b) 100 percent of the highest 15-minute demand measured in the preceding eleven months. Because of this ratchet, a load that adds to the campus peak adds to the billing demand of every month of the year.
P07: 3. Optional riders not elected
P08: Time-of-use rider TOU-2 (on-peak energy $0.1184 per kWh from 3 pm to 8 pm on summer weekdays, off-peak $0.0561 per kWh) is available to this customer class but has NOT been elected for the campus, and the campus is not eligible to elect it before 2029. It does not apply to this analysis.
P09: 4. Price forecast
P10: The Company does not publish a forecast of its rates for use in customer life-cycle cost analyses. Customers subject to federal life-cycle costing rules should apply the escalation those rules prescribe.

P00: WT-01 Condenser Water Treatment Programme Memorandum
P01: Papago Federal Center | Revision 1, 14 August 2026 | Prepared by Verde Basin Water Technologies, Inc. for the Engineer of Record
P02: 1. Supply
P03: Condenser water makeup for all three plants is Class A+ reclaimed water delivered by the municipal purveyor from the reclamation facility, at the allocation and discharge limits of letter PW-LTR-014. The supply is the same for the three plants.
P04: 2. Analysis of record
P05: The analysis of record for the supply is the most recent COMPLETE analysis in the Water Quality Portal result set in the project library, where a complete analysis is one that reports dissolved calcium, dissolved alkalinity, total dissolved solids in mg/L, dissolved sulfate and dissolved silica from the same sampling date. Field-parameter-only visits are not complete analyses. Earlier complete analyses in the same result set are superseded by the most recent one and must not be used for the selection.
P06: Calcium is reported in the result set as mg/L as Ca. Calcium hardness as CaCO3 is the reported dissolved calcium multiplied by 2.497. The 'Hardness, Ca, Mg' result is total hardness and includes magnesium; it is not calcium hardness and must not be used in the indices. Where a determinand is reported both as dissolved and as recoverable, the dissolved result is used. Results reported in tons per acre-foot or tons per day are loading figures, not concentrations. Where total dissolved solids is reported in mg/L both as measured residue on evaporation and as a value computed from the constituents, the measured residue on evaporation is the value of record.
P07: 3. Programme
P08: The programme is a phosphonate and polymer stabilised alkaline programme with sulphuric acid feed. The acid feed holds the circulating M-alkalinity at 120 ppm as CaCO3 at all cycles of concentration; alkalinity therefore does not cycle up. Total dissolved solids and calcium hardness cycle up in proportion to the cycles of concentration. A conductivity controller with an automatic blowdown valve and metering pumps for the inhibitor and the biocide are required at every plant, as is a makeup water meter.
P09: 4. Controlling cycles of concentration
P10: The allowable cycles of concentration are the lowest of the limits the adopted water treatment manual gives for the scale-forming salts that this programme does not address, and the limit that the calcium carbonate scaling index of the same manual permits. The inhibitor package addresses calcium carbonate AND calcium sulfate, so neither the manual's rough calcium carbonate prediction nor its calcium sulfate prediction is a controlling limit here; calcium phosphate is not applicable because the circulating orthophosphate is held below 10 ppm by the programme. Silica is not addressed by the programme and its limit applies as the manual states it.
P11: The programme is qualified by the supplier to a computed Practical (Puckorius) Scaling Index of not less than 5.60. Below that value the dispersant cannot hold calcium carbonate in solution and the programme is not warranted. The index is evaluated at the hottest waterside temperature of the system, which for these plants is the condenser water return temperature at the design point - the return temperature the selected cells actually produce there (the CWR the calculation workbook's design point sheet reports), not a scheduled figure - and at the circulating concentrations that the selected cycles of concentration produce.
P12: 4.1 Evaluation of the index factors
P13: Factor B is taken from the manual's temperature table by linear interpolation. Factors A, C and D are the closed forms that the manual's tables tabulate, adopted here so that the index can be evaluated where the circulating concentration leaves the tabulated range:
P14:     A = (log10(total dissolved solids in ppm) - 1) / 10
P15:     C = log10(calcium hardness as CaCO3 in ppm) - 0.4
P16:     D = log10(M-alkalinity as CaCO3 in ppm)
P17: These reproduce the manual's tables across their whole tabulated range. The equilibrium pH is the closed form the manual's appendix gives as an alternative to its chart.
P18: 5. Other limits
P19: Circulating pH is controlled to 8.0 to 8.6. The blowdown discharged to the sanitary sewer must not exceed the daily limit of PW-LTR-014. Legionella control follows the campus water management plan and does not change the water balance.
P20: 6. Programme cost
P21: The programme is supplied as a full-service contract: inhibitor, dispersant, biocide, sulphuric acid, controller service and monthly testing, billed at $0.42 per 1,000 gallons of makeup water treated, at prices in effect on 1 October 2025. The contract price is adjusted for general inflation only.
================================================================================

P00: SECTION 23 25 00 - HVAC WATER TREATMENT (EXCERPT)
P01: Papago Federal Center | Excerpt issued with the bid set for reference, 14 August 2026
P02: EXCERPT. This section covers the CLOSED hydronic systems of the project. The condenser water (open evaporative) treatment programme is specified in the water treatment memorandum WT-01 and is not covered by this section.
P03: 2.1 Closed loop chilled water and heating hot water
P04: Provide a nitrite-molybdate closed system inhibitor at 800 to 1,200 ppm as nitrite, with a tolyltriazole yellow metal inhibitor at 5 to 10 ppm. Maintain closed system pH between 8.5 and 10.5. Closed systems do not concentrate and have no cycles of concentration, no blowdown and no evaporative makeup.
P05: 2.2 Glycol
P06: Where freeze protection is required, use inhibited propylene glycol at 30 percent by volume, with a freeze point of -13 deg F and a burst point of -60 deg F. Ethylene glycol is prohibited. Correct the pump head and the heat transfer capacity for the glycol properties at the operating temperature: at 30 percent propylene glycol the specific heat is 0.90 and the specific gravity is 1.02 at 100 deg F, so the flow required for a given duty and range increases by approximately 9 percent.
P07: 2.3 Glycol feed
P08: Provide a 55 gallon glycol feed unit with a pressure switch, a low level alarm and a backflow preventer for each closed system requiring glycol.

P00: PW-LTR-014 Reclaimed Water Allocation and Discharge Limits
P01: Papago Municipal Water and Wastewater Authority | 3 July 2026 | to the General Services Administration, Papago Federal Center
P02: This letter confirms the reclaimed water allocation available to the Papago Federal Center for evaporative heat rejection makeup, and the limits on the discharge of cooling tower blowdown to the sanitary sewer, for the condenser water heat rejection replacement project.
P03: 1. Allocation
P04: The per-plant allocations above are firm. They are not transferable between plants and they are not increased by the campus total. An allocation covers all makeup water drawn by that plant: evaporation, drift and blowdown.
P05: 2. Peak day
P06: The peak day allocation is tested as twenty-four hours of continuous operation at the plant's design day condition, with the plant controlled as scheduled. The design day condition is the design outdoor wet-bulb temperature, the design block load, and - for a water balance that needs the state of the air rather than only its wet bulb - the highest outdoor dry-bulb temperature the block load schedule tabulates for that plant, which is the dry bulb the design block load is reached at.
P07: 3. Discharge
P08: Cooling tower blowdown may be discharged to the sanitary sewer up to the daily limit tabulated above. The limit is tested on the same peak day basis as paragraph 2. Discharge above the limit requires a separate industrial discharge permit, which the Authority will not issue for this facility.
P09: 4. Metering
P10: Each plant must be separately metered on the makeup line and on the blowdown line. Meter readings are reported to the Authority monthly.
P11: 5. Rates
P12: Reclaimed water delivered for evaporative heat rejection makeup is billed at $1.94 per 1,000 gallons of metered makeup. Cooling tower blowdown discharged to the sanitary sewer is billed at $3.20 per 1,000 gallons of metered blowdown. These are the rates in effect on 1 October 2025.
P13: For planning purposes the Authority forecasts that both rates will increase by 3.5 percent per year in then-current dollars over the next thirty years. The forecast is the Authority's financial plan and includes general inflation.

def eval_full_plant(plant_name, model_name, n_cells, gpm_total, cws_min_F, cws_offset_F, coc_override=None, eliminator="DE-2", material="SS-304", evap_method="LOSS-FACTOR", e_water_mode="exact"):
    ch = CHILLERS[plant_name]
    tw = TOWERS[model_name]
    rf = ROOFS[plant_name]
    N_ch = ch["N"]
    T_chw_C = (ch["T_chw_F"] - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
    gpm_eff_nom = tw["gpm_nom"] * (1.15 if model_name.endswith("-H") else 1.0)
    gpm_eff_min = max(tw["gpm_min"], 0.75 * gpm_eff_nom)
    gpm_eff_max = min(tw["gpm_max"], 1.25 * gpm_eff_nom)
    min_afr = 0.30
    free_conv_frac = 0.125
    high_speed_fan_kW_cell = (tw["bhp"] * 0.7457) / ((tw["eff_prem"] / 100.0) * 0.97)
    drift_frac = {"DE-1": 0.005, "DE-2": 0.002, "DE-3": 0.0005}[eliminator] / 100.0

    def chiller_perf_at_cws(load_tons, cws_F, n_ch_override=None):
        cws_C = (cws_F - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
        capft = eval_biquad(ch["CAPFT"], T_chw_C, cws_C)
        avail_cap_tons = ch["RefCap_tons"] * capft
        avail_cap_W = ch["RefCap_W"] * capft
        if n_ch_override is not None:
            n_on = n_ch_override
        else:
            n_on = N_ch
            for k in range(1, N_ch + 1):
                if k * avail_cap_tons >= load_tons:
                    n_on = k
                    break
        load_per_ch_tons = load_tons / n_on
        plr_raw = min(load_per_ch_tons / avail_cap_tons, ch["MaxPLR"])
        plr = max(plr_raw, ch["MinUnload"])
        frac = min(1.0, plr_raw / ch["MinPLR"]) if plr_raw < ch["MinPLR"] else 1.0
        eirft = eval_biquad(ch["EIRFT"], T_chw_C, cws_C)
        eirfplr = eval_quad(ch["EIRFPLR"], plr)
        ch_kW = n_on * (avail_cap_W / 1000.0 / ch["RefCOP"]) * eirft * eirfplr * frac
        q_evap_W = load_tons * 3516.8525
        q_cond_W = q_evap_W + ch_kW * 1000.0
        q_cond_BTUH = q_cond_W * 3.412141633
        return n_on, avail_cap_tons, ch_kW, q_cond_W, q_cond_BTUH, load_per_ch_tons / avail_cap_tons

    def pump_kW_fn(n_ch_on, cw_flow_gpm):
        p = ch["Pump"]
        q_pump = cw_flow_gpm / n_ch_on
        ratio2 = (q_pump / p["Q_ref"]) ** 2
        H_ft = p["H_static"] + (p["H_pipe"] + p["H_cond"]) * ratio2
        P_Pump_kW = (q_pump * H_ft * 0.7457) / (3960.0 * p["eta_p"] * p["eta_m"])
        return n_ch_on * P_Pump_kW

    def get_cells_on(cw_flow_gpm, n_cells_avail):
        c_on = n_cells_avail
        while c_on > 1 and (cw_flow_gpm / c_on) < gpm_eff_min:
            c_on -= 1
        return c_on

    # 1. Design Point
    Twb_des_F = 80.0
    Twb_des_C = (Twb_des_F - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
    wfr_des = (gpm_total / n_cells) / gpm_eff_nom

    def des_res(cws_F):
        _, _, _, _, q_cond_BTUH, _ = chiller_perf_at_cws(ch["DesignLoad_tons"], cws_F, n_ch_override=N_ch)
        range_F = q_cond_BTUH / (500.0 * gpm_total)
        tr_C = range_F * 5.0 / 9.0
        ta_C = york_approach_C(wfr_des, 1.0, Twb_des_C, tr_C)
        return (Twb_des_F + ta_C * 9.0 / 5.0) - cws_F

    cws_des_F = brentq(des_res, 60.0, 125.0, xtol=1e-6)
    _, avail_des_tons, ch_des_kW, q_cond_des_W, q_cond_des_BTUH, plr_des = chiller_perf_at_cws(ch["DesignLoad_tons"], cws_des_F, n_ch_override=N_ch)
    range_des_F = q_cond_des_BTUH / (500.0 * gpm_total)
    approach_des_F = cws_des_F - Twb_des_F
    cwr_des_F = cws_des_F + range_des_F

    max_coc = get_max_coc(cwr_des_F)
    if coc_override is not None:
        coc = coc_override
    else:
        coc = math.floor(max_coc * 100.0) / 100.0
    psi_des = calc_PSI(coc, cwr_des_F)

    # 2. Redundancy (Twb_red_F = 81.0 F -> TwbCapped_C = 26.6667 C)
    Twb_red_F = 81.0
    Twb_red_cap_C = 26.6667 # clamped at 80 F (26.6667 C)
    # Case A: N_ch - 1 chillers, n_cells available
    n_ch_A = N_ch - 1
    cw_A = (n_ch_A / N_ch) * gpm_total
    c_on_A = get_cells_on(cw_A, n_cells)
    wfr_A = (cw_A / c_on_A) / gpm_eff_nom
    def red_eq(cws_F, n_ch_case, cw_case, wfr_case, twb_base_F):
        cws_C = (cws_F - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
        capft = eval_biquad(ch["CAPFT"], T_chw_C, cws_C)
        cap_tons = n_ch_case * ch["RefCap_tons"] * capft
        _, _, _, _, q_btuh, _ = chiller_perf_at_cws(cap_tons, cws_F, n_ch_override=n_ch_case)
        rng_F = q_btuh / (500.0 * cw_case)
        ta_C = york_approach_C(wfr_case, 1.0, Twb_red_cap_C, rng_F * 5.0 / 9.0)
        return (twb_base_F + ta_C * 9.0 / 5.0) - cws_F

    cws_A_81 = brentq(lambda x: red_eq(x, n_ch_A, cw_A, wfr_A, 81.0), 60.0, 125.0, xtol=1e-6)
    cap_A_81 = n_ch_A * ch["RefCap_tons"] * eval_biquad(ch["CAPFT"], T_chw_C, (cws_A_81 - 32.0)*5.0/9.0)

    # Case B: n_cells - 1 available
    c_avail_B = n_cells - 1
    if (gpm_total / c_avail_B) > gpm_eff_max:
        n_ch_B = N_ch - 1
        cw_B = (n_ch_B / N_ch) * gpm_total
    else:
        n_ch_B = N_ch
        cw_B = gpm_total
    c_on_B = get_cells_on(cw_B, c_avail_B)
    wfr_B = (cw_B / c_on_B) / gpm_eff_nom
    cws_B_81 = brentq(lambda x: red_eq(x, n_ch_B, cw_B, wfr_B, 81.0), 60.0, 125.0, xtol=1e-6)
    cap_B_81 = n_ch_B * ch["RefCap_tons"] * eval_biquad(ch["CAPFT"], T_chw_C, (cws_B_81 - 32.0)*5.0/9.0)

    red_cap_tons = min(cap_A_81, cap_B_81)
    red_cws_max_F = max(cws_A_81, cws_B_81)

    # 3. Peak Day Water Balance (24 hours at Twb = 80.0 F, Tdb = 112.0 F, Load = DesignLoad_tons, controlled as scheduled)
    t_set_pk_F = max(cws_min_F, 80.0 + cws_offset_F)
    if cws_des_F >= t_set_pk_F:
        cws_pk_F = cws_des_F
        q_cond_pk_W = q_cond_des_W
        rng_pk_F = range_des_F
        afr_pk = 1.0
    else:
        cws_pk_F = t_set_pk_F
        _, _, _, q_cond_pk_W, q_cond_pk_BTUH, _ = chiller_perf_at_cws(ch["DesignLoad_tons"], cws_pk_F, n_ch_override=N_ch)
        rng_pk_F = q_cond_pk_BTUH / (500.0 * gpm_total)
        tr_pk_C = rng_pk_F * 5.0 / 9.0
        ta_pk_C = (cws_pk_F - 80.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
        ta_min_pk_C = york_approach_C(wfr_des, min_afr, Twb_des_C, tr_pk_C)
        if ta_min_pk_C >= ta_pk_C:
            afr_pk = brentq(lambda a: york_approach_C(wfr_des, a, Twb_des_C, tr_pk_C) - ta_pk_C, min_afr, 1.0, xtol=1e-6)
        else:
            afr_pk = min_afr

    if evap_method == "LOSS-FACTOR":
        evap_pk_gpm = 0.001 * gpm_total * rng_pk_F
    else:
        wb_pk_C = (80.0 - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
        db_pk_C = (112.0 - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0
        hum_pk = PsyWFnTdbTwbPb(db_pk_C, wb_pk_C, P_atm_Pa)
        rho_pk = PsyRhoAirFnPbTdbW(P_atm_Pa, db_pk_C, hum_pk)
        m_air_pk = afr_pk * (tw["cfm"] * 0.00047194745) * n_cells * rho_pk
        h_in_pk = PsyHFnTdbRhPb(wb_pk_C, 1.0, P_atm_Pa)
        h_out_pk = h_in_pk + q_cond_pk_W / m_air_pk

Condenser Water Heat Rejection Replacement. Submittal date 24 July 2026, revision 1.

78 deg F entering wet bulb, at design air flow. The nominal water flow is the reference flow of the variable speed
performance object used to model the cell, so the water flow rate ratio of that object is the actual flow through the cell
divided by the nominal flow in this table. Thermal capability is certified under CTI STD-201 for the whole range.

The -S casing is the standard casing. The -H casing is the high efficiency casing: deeper fill and a larger plan area for the
same nominal water flow, with a smaller fan for the same thermal duty. Thermal capability at a given water flow rate ratio
and air flow rate ratio is identical for the two casings of one nominal size; the -H casing reaches its design air flow with less
fan power and occupies more roof area and more weight.
The operating weight is the weight to be carried by the supporting structure with the basin at its operating level and the cell
in service. The plan dimension is the plan of the support frame, which is the area over which the operating weight is
distributed.
3. Water flow limits
The minimum and maximum water flows above are the distribution basin's wetting and flooding limits. They are limits on the
equipment. The performance object used to model the cell carries its own water flow rate ratio limits, and both apply.

3. Condenser water flow limits
The minimum flow is the tube velocity limit below which fouling and laminar transition occur; the maximum flow is the
erosion velocity limit. Both are per machine. The condenser pressure drop varies with the square of the flow.
4. Part load
Capacity, electric input ratio and part load behaviour are entirely defined by the curves of the named performance data set.
No separate part load table is issued with this submittal.

P00: DC-02 Mechanical Design Criteria Memorandum - Condenser Water Heat Rejection
P01: Papago Federal Center, Phoenix, Arizona | Revision 3, 14 August 2026 | Sandoval Klee Mechanical Engineers, PC
This memorandum supersedes DC-02 Revision 2 in its entirety. Revision 3 adds the life-cycle cost objective (paragraph 4, EC-01) and the LifeCycleCost sheet of Appendix A.2.
P02: 1. Scope
P03: This memorandum states the criteria, conventions and deliverable requirements for the replacement of the condenser water heat rejection plants serving the Courthouse Central Utility Plant (CUP), the Data Annex (ANNEX) and the Laboratory Wing (LAB). The chillers, the condenser water pumps' hydraulic circuits and the electrical distribution are existing or already procured and are not in the scope of this design.
P04: 2. Adopted criteria
P05: 3. Plants and served loads
P06: Block cooling loads as a function of outdoor dry-bulb temperature are scheduled on M-603. Chiller performance data and condenser water limits are on M-601 and submittal VD-03.
P07: 4. Objective
P08: Each plant must be designed for the HIGHEST LIFE-CYCLE NET SAVINGS, relative to the basic design, consistent with every requirement of the adopted criteria and of this memorandum, with the life-cycle cost analysis performed as EC-01 directs under 10 CFR Part 436 Subpart A. It is not the design with the lowest energy, nor the one with the lowest first cost, unless the analysis makes it so.
P09: Annual plant electrical energy - the energy quantity the analysis prices - is the sum over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 of the bin hours multiplied by the coincident electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps of that plant.
P10: 5. Climatic and property basis
P11: 5.1 Governing station
P12: The climatic basis is the National Centers for Environmental Information Local Climatological Data record of the airport station serving the site, for the three complete calendar years in the project library. That record is the period of record (POR) for every percentile in this memorandum. Only observations whose report type is FM-15 or FM-16 are counted; the daily and monthly summary rows of the record are not observations. Records for any other station in the library are not part of the POR.
P13: 5.2 Design outdoor conditions
P14: A percentile design value is the value that was exceeded that percentage of the observations over the entire POR, taken as a single annual population (not a seasonal one). The design outdoor wet-bulb temperature for the heat rejection equipment is the 1.0 percent annual wet-bulb temperature so computed, adjusted as the adopted HVAC criteria require for open cooling towers. The failure-case calculation of paragraph 6.3 uses the wet-bulb basis that the adopted agency facilities standard prescribes for evaporative machines, adjusted the same way. Do not take design values from the cancelled weather-data criteria document.
P15: 5.3 Scenario bins
P16: Annual performance is evaluated on scenario bins formed from the POR observations: bin each observation by wet-bulb temperature in 2 deg F bins and by dry-bulb temperature in 5 deg F bins, take the bin condition as the bin mid-points, and scale the bin counts so that the bins total 8760 hours per year. The block load of a bin is the M-603 load at the bin dry-bulb temperature. Where a bin's dry-bulb mid-point would fall below its wet-bulb mid-point, the dry-bulb temperature is taken equal to the wet-bulb mid-point. The bin edges fall at whole multiples of the bin width measured from zero deg F: an observation belongs to the bin whose lower edge is the largest such multiple that does not exceed it, the lower edge belonging to the bin and the upper edge to the next one, so that a bin's mid-point is its lower edge plus half the bin width.
P17: 5.4 Freeze protection
P18: A basin heater and heat-traced makeup piping are required only where the 99.6 percent annual dry-bulb temperature computed from the POR is at or below 32 deg F. The design basis must state the computed 99.6 percent dry-bulb temperature and the determination that follows from it.
P19: 5.5 Property basis
P20: Moist air properties are those of the psychrometric routines of the reference implementation in the project library (saturation pressure over water, humidity ratio from dry- and wet-bulb, moist air enthalpy and density, and saturation temperature from enthalpy). The barometric pressure is the mean station pressure of the governing POR, not a sea-level or a standard-atmosphere value. Water is taken at 8.33 lb/gal and 1.0 BTU/lb-deg F, so that heat rejection in BTU/h is 500 times the flow in gpm times the range in deg F.
P21: 6. Plant configuration and operating conventions
P22: 6.1 Cells and controls
P23: All cells of a plant are of one model and one size and carry identical fan, motor, drift eliminator and material selections. Every tower fan motor is driven by a variable frequency drive. The number of cells must be a whole multiple of the number of chillers served.
P24: 6.2 Condenser water flow
P25: Each chiller has a dedicated constant-speed condenser water pump. The scheduled design flow is the flow with every chiller running; the flow with n chillers running is n/N of it. The per-chiller flow must lie inside the condenser flow limits of submittal VD-03 and the per-cell flow inside the limits of submittal VD-01.
P26: 6.3 Redundancy
P27: The plant must meet its design block load with the largest single cell out of service, at the failure-case wet-bulb basis of paragraph 5.2, with the remaining cells at full fan speed, and at an entering condenser water temperature no warmer than the machines' published maximum (submittal VD-03). This is the cooling robustness performance tier the agency facilities standard requires.
P28: With a cell out of service the design condenser water flow is unchanged - every chiller is still running on its dedicated constant-speed pump (paragraph 6.2) - and it is carried by the cells that remain in service. The flow through each remaining cell in that state must lie inside the per-cell flow limits of submittal VD-01 and inside the water flow rate ratio limits of the performance object (paragraph 6.8). A plant whose remaining cells would have to pass more than that does not meet this requirement, whatever temperature a calculation extrapolated beyond those limits might predict: a cell above its rated distribution capacity and outside the validity envelope of its performance model has no substantiated capability. The clamping described in the second part of paragraph 6.8 applies to the inlet wet-bulb temperature only; it does not apply to the water flow rate ratio, in this case or any other.
P29: 6.4 Condenser water pump power
P30: Condenser water pump total head is taken as a fixed static lift plus a friction component that varies with the square of the flow ratio:
P31:     H = H_static + (H_pipe + H_condenser) x (Q / Q_ref)^2        [ft of water]
P32:     Pump shaft power = Q x H / (3960 x eta_pump)                 [hp, Q in gpm]
P33:     Pump electrical input = shaft power x 0.7457 / eta_motor     [kW]
P34: where Q is the flow through one pump. The per-plant constants are:
P35: 6.5 Chiller staging
P36: Chillers stage on in order: the smallest number of machines whose available capacity at the operating leaving chilled water and entering condenser water temperatures meets the block load runs, and the load is divided equally between them.
P37: Available capacity here is the capacity the adopted performance data set makes available at those temperatures: the machine's reference capacity multiplied by its capacity-as-a-function-of-temperature curve evaluated at the operating point, and nothing else. The maximum part load ratio is not part of available capacity. It is a separate published limit - the ceiling on the load a machine that is already running may be given - and it is not applied to the capacity that decides how many machines run.
P38: 6.6 Cell staging
P39: Condenser water is distributed to every installed cell unless the resulting per-cell flow would fall below the effective minimum, which is the larger of the submittal's minimum per-cell flow and the flow at which the performance object's minimum water flow rate ratio is reached. Cells are then isolated one at a time until the per-cell flow is at or above the effective minimum. Tower fans of the cells in service modulate together.
P40: 6.7 Condenser water supply temperature control
P41: The condenser water supply temperature setpoint is scheduled as a wet-bulb-following reset: the setpoint is the larger of a scheduled floor and the outdoor wet-bulb temperature plus a scheduled offset, and is in no case below the minimum entering condenser water temperature the chillers are rated for. The fans modulate to the setpoint exactly as the reference implementation models a variable speed tower: full speed when the setpoint cannot be met, free convection when the fans are not needed, minimum speed with cycling below that. A condenser water bypass valve holds the setpoint when the tower would otherwise overcool, so the supply temperature never falls below the setpoint.
P42: 6.8 Validity of the performance correlation
P43: A cell may not be operated at a water flow rate ratio outside the limits stated in the performance object, because the implementation clamps the ratio there and the capability would not be substantiated. The range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits of the same object apply at every scenario. A design that operates outside them is not accepted.
P44: The inlet air wet-bulb temperature is treated differently, and deliberately. The reference implementation clamps it to the object's stated range before evaluating the correlation, so an outdoor wet bulb at or above the object's maximum is evaluated AT that maximum and is never extrapolated. The design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 lands on that maximum at this site. That is not an error and no work-around is required: it is what the adopted simulation basis does, and the wet-bulb limit is therefore not one of the envelope limits this paragraph tests.
P45: 6.9 Design point
P46: At the design outdoor wet bulb of paragraph 5.2 and the design block load, with every chiller running at the scheduled design flow and the cells in service at full fan speed, the cells must deliver condenser water no warmer than the scheduled design supply temperature (CWSDESIGN), and the chillers must carry the design block load at that entering condenser water temperature. The validity limits of paragraph 6.8 - the water flow rate ratio limits, and the range, approach and liquid-to-gas ratio limits - apply at this design point as they do at every scenario. A schedule may be conservative: a CWSDESIGN warmer than the selected cells actually need is acceptable.
P47: 6.10 Peak coincident demand
P48: The peak coincident electrical demand of a plant is the largest total electrical demand of the chillers, the tower fans and the condenser water pumps operating together, taken over the scenario bins of paragraph 5.3 and over nothing else. It is a maximum over those bins, not a design-day figure: neither the design point of paragraph 6.9 nor the redundancy case of paragraph 6.3 is a scenario bin - they are sizing conditions - and neither enters this maximum. Basin heaters, controls and lighting are not part of it. This is the quantity the motor control centre's spare capacity limits and the quantity the calculation workbook reports.
P49: 7. Water
P50: The water balance, the cycles of concentration and the treatment programme are governed by the adopted water treatment manual and by the reclaimed water correspondence and treatment memorandum in the project library.
P51: Two evaporation formulations are adopted for this project, and they are these two, named so that the choice is between two fully specified methods:
P52:   SATURATED-EXIT - the moist-air method of the reference implementation's tower water-use routine: the outlet air is saturated at the inlet enthalpy plus the water-side heat transfer divided by the air mass flow, and the evaporated mass is the air mass flow times the rise in specific humidity, converted to a volume with the density of water. As the routine computes them, the inlet enthalpy is that of saturated air at the inlet wet-bulb temperature, and the water density is taken at the mean of the inlet dry-bulb and the saturated outlet air temperatures, not below 4 deg C. The routine reads that density from fluid property tables that are not part of the shipped source; on this project it is taken as rho = 1000 x (1 - (T + 288.9414) / (508929.2 x (T + 68.12963)) x (T - 3.9863)^2) kg/m3, T in deg C. Every other quantity the method needs is in the shipped source and its header.
P53:   LOSS-FACTOR - the rule of thumb of the adopted water treatment manual's cooling tower chapter, with the constant and the temperature basis that chapter states and its own worked example confirms. It is NOT the reference implementation's user-factor path: that path reads a loss factor from an input field this project does not set, and the input dictionary that would supply a default for it is not part of the adopted basis.
P54: Either may be used. The design basis must state which one was used, and the water balance of the submitted workbook must be computed consistently with the stated choice throughout.
P55: 8. Deliverable
P56: For each plant P in {CUP, ANNEX, LAB} deliver CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf and CT_CALC_P.xlsx, and once for the package constraint_register.csv and design_basis.md. Appendix A fixes the formats.
P57: 9. Design basis content
P58: The design basis must state, for each plant, the governing constraint on the design in the form:
P59:     GOVERNING CONSTRAINT <plant>: <name> (relative margin <value>)
P60: where <name> is exactly one of the following six, and is the one with the smallest relative margin at the submitted design, and <value> is that relative margin:
P61: The six names above are the only admissible values of <name>. Where two of them are within 0.004 of each other at the submitted design, either may be stated.
P62: The margins are judged against the quantities the calculation workbook reports, not against a figure to a precision the workbook cannot carry. A relative margin is a small difference divided by a limit, so it is far more sensitive than the quantity it is computed from: near a limit, a 1 percent difference in peak demand can move the margin by more than half its value. The stated margin is therefore accepted when it agrees, within 0.004, with the margin computed from the workbook's own reported peak coincident demand, annual makeup and design supply temperature - provided each of those reported quantities is itself within the tolerance the calculation checks apply to it (peak demand and annual makeup within 10 percent of the recomputed values, supply temperature within the larger of 0.8 deg F and 10 percent of the approach). A reported quantity outside its tolerance is replaced by the recomputed value. The name is accepted when it is the smallest of the six margins so computed, with the same 0.004 tie. The roof area, structural and condenser flow margins depend only on published data and the schedule, so they are computed exactly.
P63: The design basis must also state which weather basis was applied and the clause that requires it, and which evaporation formulation was used.
P64: 9.1 Documented conflicts
P65: The project library contains documents that do not agree with one another. Paragraph 2 resolves several of those disagreements directly. The design basis must record how each of the three conflicts below was resolved, one line each, in the form below; these are the three this memorandum requires a line for, not a complete list of every place the library's documents differ:
P66:     CONFLICT <n>: ADOPTED <document> <clause> | SET ASIDE <document> <clause>
P67: where <document> is the designation the document gives itself and <clause> is the paragraph, table or revision within it. The three conflicts, in this order:
P68: A conflict is resolved by naming the document and clause that governs and the document and clause that does not. Both sides must be named. The grader reads these lines; it does not read prose around them.
P69: Appendix A - Deliverable formats
P70: A.1 CT_SCHEDULE_P.dxf
P71: Plan units are feet, in the coordinates of M-401. Three layers are read:
P72:   M-CTWR-SCHD - one TEXT or MTEXT entity per scheduled field, written as '<TAG> <KEY> <VALUE>'. TAG is CT-1 ... CT-n for the cell rows and PLANT for the plant rows. Values are plain numbers or the listed keywords; units are not written into the value.
P73: MOTOREFF is the nominal full-load efficiency in percent. DRIFT is the drift rate in percent of design water flow. COC is the cycles of concentration the plant is controlled to. BASINCLR is the clear dimension in feet between the top of the roof and the underside of the tower basin. EVAPMETHOD is SATURATED-EXIT or LOSS-FACTOR. BASINHEATER, BLOWDOWNCTRL and EQUALIZING are YES or NO.
P74:   GPM is the flow through one cell with every installed cell in service, that is GPMTOTAL divided by CELLS. Where the staging rule of paragraph 6.6 leaves a cell out of service at some operating point, the scheduled figure does not change; the flow actually in each cell at each scenario belongs in the off-design table.
P75:   M-CTWR-PLAN - one closed LWPOLYLINE per cell, the rectangular plan outline of that cell's support frame, in the plan coordinates of M-401, which places the three plants on one sheet each on its own origin. One polyline per installed cell, no more and no fewer.
P76:   G-TBLK - the title block, including the sheet revision.
P77: A.2 CT_CALC_P.xlsx
P78: Five sheets. DesignPoint, WaterBalance, Energy and LifeCycleCost are two-column key/value sheets with the key in column A and the value in column B. OffDesign is a table with a header row.
P79: Values are numbers, not text with units, and no cell may be left blank or carry a placeholder.
P80: RedundancyCapacity_tons is the total cooling capacity the plant's chillers can deliver with the largest tower cell out of service, evaluated at the failure-case wet bulb of paragraph 6.3 with the remaining cells at full fan speed, at the entering condenser water temperature those remaining cells actually produce at that wet bulb and at the scheduled condenser water flow. It is the capacity available at that operating point, not the capacity available at the machine's rated maximum entering condenser water temperature, and not the reference capacity of the performance data set. It is available capacity in the sense of paragraph 6.5, so the maximum part load ratio is not applied to it. RedundancyWetBulb_F is the wet bulb it is evaluated at.
P81: LifeCycleCost: DiscountRate is the real discount rate as a fraction or in percent. StudyPeriod_yr and ConstructionPeriod_yr are in years from the base date. UPVStarElectricity, UPVStarWater and UPVNonFuel are the present-value factors the analysis multiplies the base-year annual electricity cost, water and sewer cost, and non-fuel operation and maintenance cost by, to give their present values at the base date over the period in which they accrue. P02: Question 1
P03: The Laboratory Wing exhaust fan replacement, a separate contract, connects new exhaust fan motors to MCC-R3 before the heat rejection plant is commissioned. Each fan is driven by a 7.5 hp, 4 pole, totally enclosed fan cooled motor with a nominal full-load efficiency of 91.7 percent, through a variable frequency drive with an efficiency of 0.97 at rated load. The fans serve fume hood exhaust and run continuously at full speed and full nameplate load, so they operate coincident with the heat rejection plant at every hour of the year. Add their electrical input to the retained existing demand of MCC-R3 and reduce the spare capacity available to the new heat rejection plant accordingly. The bus rating and the continuous loading limit stated on E-601 are unchanged.

P00: PW-LTR-014 Reclaimed Water Allocation and Discharge Limits
P01: Papago Municipal Water and Wastewater Authority | 3 July 2026 | to the General Services Administration, Papago Federal Center
P02: This letter confirms the reclaimed water allocation available to the Papago Federal Center for evaporative heat rejection makeup, and the limits on the discharge of cooling tower blowdown to the sanitary sewer, for the condenser water heat rejection replacement project.
P03: 1. Allocation
P04: The per-plant allocations above are firm. They are not transferable between plants and they are not increased by the campus total. An allocation covers all makeup water drawn by that plant: evaporation, drift and blowdown.
P05: 2. Peak day
P06: The peak day allocation is tested as twenty-four hours of continuous operation at the plant's design day condition, with the plant controlled as scheduled. The design day condition is the design outdoor wet-bulb temperature, the design block load, and - for a water balance that needs the state of the air rather than only its wet bulb - the highest outdoor dry-bulb temperature the block load schedule tabulates for that plant, which is the dry bulb the design block load is reached at.
P07: 3. Discharge
P08: Cooling tower blowdown may be discharged to the sanitary sewer up to the daily limit tabulated above. The limit is tested on the same peak day basis as paragraph 2. Discharge above the limit requires a separate industrial discharge permit, which the Authority will not issue for this facility.
P09: 4. Metering
P10: Each plant must be separately metered on the makeup line and on the blowdown line. Meter readings are reported to the Authority monthly.
P11: 5. Rates
P12: Reclaimed water delivered for evaporative heat rejection makeup is billed at $1.94 per 1,000 gallons of metered makeup. Cooling tower blowdown discharged to the sanitary sewer is billed at $3.20 per 1,000 gallons of metered blowdown. These are the rates in effect on 1 October 2025.
P13: For planning purposes the Authority forecasts that both rates will increase by 3.5 percent per year in then-current dollars over the next thirty years. The forecast is the Authority's financial plan and includes general inflation.

CHAPTER 2 INTRODUCTION TO INDUSTRIAL WATER TREATMENT 
2-1 
INDUSTRIAL WATER TREATMENT. 
Industrial water is not the same as potable water. Industrial water is never consumed or 
used under situations that require a high degree of sanitation. 
Industrial water requires water preparation or chemical treatment, or both, to avoid the 
problems described in paragraph 2-1.2. Water preparation and chemical treatment 
requirements are described in Chapters 3 through 6 according to the type of system in 
question.  The shore-to-ship steam purity standards are described in Chapter 4. 
Examples of industrial water systems and their uses are: 
• 
Steam Boiler Systems. (See Chapter 4.) Steam uses include space and 
hot water heating, sterilization, humidification, indirect food processing, 
and power generation. 
• 
Cooling Water Systems. (See Chapter 5.)  Cooling water is used in 
cooling towers, evaporative coolers, evaporative condensers, and once- 
through systems. Applications are broad, ranging from simple refrigeration 
to temperature regulation of nuclear reactors. 
• 
Closed Water Systems. (See Chapter 6.) These include closed hot water, 
closed chilled water, and diesel jacket systems. 
2-1.1 
Fire Protection and Other Uses. 
Fire protection systems such as dedicated fire water distribution systems and building 
fire sprinkler systems are not considered industrial water systems. 
2-1.2 
Problems Encountered in Industrial Water Systems. 
Problems found in industrial water systems are attributable to reduced or restricted 
water flow or other changes in operational parameters, and often caused by corrosion, 
deposits, and biological growth. These problems result in reduced system efficiency 
(higher operating costs), increased equipment replacement costs, and reduced safety. 
At times they can be serious enough to cause complete system shutdown. The 
problems in industrial water systems fall into three main categories: 
• 
Steam boiler water problems (corrosion, deposits, and carryover). 
• 
Cooling water problems (corrosion, deposits, and biological). 
• 
Closed loop problems (corrosion, deposits, and biological). 
2-1.2.1

4-1.4.3 
Carryover Problems. 
Carryover problems are caused by misting, foaming, priming, and silica carryover (see 
paragraph 4-2.8). Carryover is a process that results in impure steam quality. Dissolved 
solids contained in the carryover material can contribute to corrosion and deposition 
problems. 
4-1.5 
Calculations. 
To understand and produce efficient boiler operations, boiler calculations are performed 
and the results applied correctly. Boiler calculations are the means for providing 
information used to determine optimal blowdown rates and to assess condensate 
return. The greatest efficiency of boiler operations can be achieved by optimizing the 
COC by adjusting the amount of blowdown to give the proper volume of water. Efficient 
boiler operations recover and return as much condensate as possible. The material 
balance or mass balance of an operating boiler system can be calculated from the 
results of water tests and the known (measured) value of a single boiler operational 
parameter such as steam production, makeup water usage, feed water usage, or 
blowdown. Steam table data can be used with mass balance information to calculate 
energy input and energy output for the boiler system. Chemical feed rates can be used 
with mass balance information to develop an estimation tool for the annual consumption 
of water treatment chemicals. Familiarity with these calculation procedures and their 
application to boiler system operations assessment is required of any base or facility 
engineer or section supervisor. This knowledge is also useful for boiler operators. 
Examples of boiler calculations are provided in paragraphs 4-1.5.3 through 4-1.6.3.

4-1.5.1 
Cycles of Concentration (COC). 
COC in a steam boiler is a term that refers to the number of times the minerals in the 
feed water have been concentrated in the boiler by its operation. As boiler water 
evaporates and steam is produced, minerals that were dissolved in the boiler water 
remain behind, increasing the mineral content of the remaining water. As steam is 
produced, additional mineral-laden feed water enters the boiler, resulting in additional 
minerals being introduced into the boiler and increasing the amount present in the 
boiler. Mineral content in an operating boiler water system can be limited only by 
blowdown. 
4-1.5.2 
Blowdown. 
Blowdown consists of draining some of the boiler water with its accumulated solids, and 
replacing it with treated feed water before harmful levels of solids are reached. 
Dissolved solids tend to concentrate near the water surface in the steam drum. 
Therefore, surface blowdown is most effective in reducing the concentration of 
dissolved solids. Bottom blowdown is used to remove precipitated sludge from the boiler

5-1.5.2 
White Rust. 
Some cooling towers are constructed with galvanized steel components and must not 
be exposed to conditions of high pH (high alkalinity). The galvanizing process deposits 
a protective zinc coating on a mild steel metal surface, resulting in increased resistance 
to corrosion. Failure to avoid such exposure can result in production of “white rust” due 
to the corrosion of the galvanizing coating. Eventually, this corrosion process exposes 
the mild steel underneath, which then starts to corrode. White rust failures have been a 
common occurrence throughout the country, mainly with newer cooling towers. Proper 
protection of the galvanizing material is necessary both during startup of a new cooling 
tower and during normal operations. Specific water treatment chemicals are needed to 
provide this protection. Examples include pretreatment with a high level of 
orthophosphate. 
5-1.5.3 
Cooling Tower Film Fill. 
Small- and medium-sized cooling towers use film fill, which is a tightly packed media as 
compared to the splash-type fill used prevalently in the past (see paragraph 5-1.4.3 and 
Figure 5-11). Film fill has a higher potential for fouling (plugging) due to adherence and 
entrapment of biomass and of SS (such as dirt, silt, and sand). The cooling capacity of a 
cooling tower can be reduced if the film fill is extensively fouled (see Figure 5-14). 
Instances of severe fouling have resulted in the collapse of fill into the cooling tower 
basin. In addition, fouling deposits in the fill can harbor pathogenic microbiological 
organisms such as Legionnaires’ disease. 

=== PDF Page 122 ===
UFM 3-230-13 
5 February 2026 
 
 
105 
Figure 5-14 Heavily Fouled Cooling Tower Film Fill 
 
5-1.5.4 
Legionella Bacteria. 
This type of bacteria is the cause of Legionnaires’ disease. It can grow in cooling water 
systems even when a proper microbiological control program has been maintained. This 
bacterium can be discharged in the drift produced from all types of cooling tower 
systems. If a susceptible person inhales the bacteria, the disease could possibly 
develop. A number of outbreaks of Legionnaires’ disease are reported throughout the 
country. See paragraph 5-4.7 for information on controlling Legionella. 
5-2 
COOLING TOWER WATER CALCULATIONS 
5-2.1 
Principles of Cooling Tower System Operations. 
The function of a cooling tower is to dissipate heat from water-cooled refrigeration, air-
conditioning and industrial process systems. Water is typically the heat transfer medium 
used to dissipate the heat. A cooling tower uses a combination of heat and mass 
transfer (evaporation) to cool the water flowing through the tower. Conductive heat 
transfer accounts for 20 to 30 percent of the total heat dissipated. The remaining 70 to 
80 percent of total cooling is the result of evaporative cooling of about 1 to 2 percent of 
the recirculating water, depending on the decrease in temperature across the tower. It 
takes approximately 2,326,000 joules to evaporate 1000 BTU per 1 pound of water (1 
kilogram of water). If this amount of heat is extracted from 1000 pounds (454 kilograms) 
of water, approximately 1 pound (0.45 kilogram) of water will be evaporated and the 
temperature will drop 1° F (0.55° C). If 10 pounds (4.5 kilograms) of water are 
evaporated, the water temperature will drop 10° F (5.5° C). The water lost by evaporation 
is replaced with makeup water. Water is also added to replace water lost through tower 
drift (loss of water from the tower as a fine mist), leaks in the system (unintentional 
blowdown), and water discharged as intentional blowdown. Water that is added to the 
cooling tower to replace all of these losses is known as cooling tower makeup water.

5-2.1.1

The operation of cooling towers can be described by the relationship between 
evaporation, blowdown, and makeup. Makeup water must equal blowdown water plus 
water evaporation to maintain a constant operating water level in the system: 
Equation 5-1. 
Operation of Cooling Towers 
MM= BB+ EE 
Where: 
M = makeup water, gpm (liters/sec) 
B = blowdown, gpm (liters/sec) (all sources) 
E = evaporation, gpm (liters/sec)

One of the common terms used in describing the water use efficiency of cooling tower 
water systems is COC. COC represents the relationship between the makeup water 
quantity and blowdown quantity. COC is a measure of the total amount of minerals that 
is concentrated in the cooling tower water relative to the amount of minerals in the 
makeup water or to the volume of each type of water. The higher the COC, the greater 
the water use efficiency. Most cooling tower systems operate with a COC of 3 to 10, 
where 3 represents acceptable efficiency and 10 represents very good efficiency. It has 
been found that the range of 5 to 7 COC represents the most cost-effective situation.

COC and makeup requirements are related to the temperature drop across a cooling 
tower and to the recirculating rate of the tower. As shown in Figure 5-15, for a

be adjusted (increased) to allow for reductions in water use (water conservation) and for 
reductions in the amount of water treatment chemicals used.

5-3 
OBJECTIVES OF COOLING WATER TREATMENT. 
The primary objectives of cooling water treatment are to maintain the operating 
efficiency of the cooling water system and to protect the equipment that contacts the 
cooling water. These objectives are accomplished by controlling or minimizing 
deposition, corrosion, and microbiological growth on the cooling water equipment. 
Treatment programs must also address requirements for environmental compliance, 
safety, water conservation, and limitation of chemical costs. This paragraph reviews the 
requirements for, and elements of, a water treatment program for cooling water 
systems. 
5-3.1 
Deposit Formation and Control. 
Deposits that occur in cooling water systems are usually divided into two categories: 
scale and fouling. The presence of either type of deposit in the heat exchangers or in 
the film fill can interfere with heat transfer, thereby reducing the efficiency of operation. 
Deposits can also promote under- deposit corrosion. Scale and non-biological fouling 
are described in this paragraph. Biological fouling is described in paragraph 5-4. 
5-3.2 
Scale. 
Scale is formed from minerals, formerly dissolved in water, that were deposited from the 
water onto heat transfer surfaces or in-flow water lines. As water is evaporated in a 
cooling tower, the concentration of dissolved solids becomes greater until the solubility 
of a particular scale-causing mineral salt is exceeded. When this situation occurs in an 
untreated cooling water system, the scale will form on any surface in contact with the 
water, especially on heat transfer surfaces. The most common scaling minerals are 
calcium carbonate, calcium phosphate, calcium sulfate, and silica, usually in that order. 
Formation of magnesium silicate scale is also possible under certain conditions. Most 
other salts, including silica, are more soluble in hot water than in cold water; however, 
most calcium and magnesium salts, including calcium phosphate and calcium 
carbonate, are more soluble in cold water than in hot water. This is called “reverse 
solubility.” The water temperature will increase as recirculating water passes through 
the cooling system. As a result, calcium and magnesium scales may form anywhere in 
the system, but most likely on heated surfaces such as heat exchangers or surface 
condensers. Silica will form in areas having the lowest water temperature, such as in 
the cooling tower fill.

The maximum solubility limit for specific dissolved minerals will determine the types of 
scale that can form under a given set of conditions. To minimize water blowdown, the 
amount of dissolved materials in the cooling water should be maintained as close as 
possible to the maximum solubility level. This water quality parameter, TDS, is 
controlled by maintaining COC in the system at a level that is equal to the lowest COC 
allowable for whichever salt has the lowest solubility. The salt of concern is often 
calcium carbonate or calcium phosphate, but it may be silica. The operating COC can 
be increased substantially with use of the cooling water treatment chemicals described 
in this paragraph.

OBJECTIVES OF COOLING WATER TREATMENT.

The primary objectives of cooling water treatment are to maintain the operating
efficiency of the cooling water system and to protect the equipment that contacts the
cooling water. These objectives are accomplished by controlling or minimizing
deposition, corrosion, and microbiological growth on the cooling water equipment.
Treatment programs must also address requirements for environmental compliance,
safety, water conservation, and limitation of chemical costs. This paragraph reviews the
requirements for, and elements of, a water treatment program for cooling water
systems.
5-3.1

Deposit Formation and Control.

Deposits that occur in cooling water systems are usually divided into two categories:
scale and fouling. The presence of either type of deposit in the heat exchangers or in
the film fill can interfere with heat transfer, thereby reducing the efficiency of operation.
Deposits can also promote under- deposit corrosion. Scale and non-biological fouling
are described in this paragraph. Biological fouling is described in paragraph 5-4.
5-3.2

Scale.

Scale is formed from minerals, formerly dissolved in water, that were deposited from the
water onto heat transfer surfaces or in-flow water lines. As water is evaporated in a
cooling tower, the concentration of dissolved solids becomes greater until the solubility
of a particular scale-causing mineral salt is exceeded. When this situation occurs in an
untreated cooling water system, the scale will form on any surface in contact with the
water, especially on heat transfer surfaces. The most common scaling minerals are
calcium carbonate, calcium phosphate, calcium sulfate, and silica, usually in that order.
Formation of magnesium silicate scale is also possible under certain conditions. Most
other salts, including silica, are more soluble in hot water than in cold water; however,
most calcium and magnesium salts, including calcium phosphate and calcium
carbonate, are more soluble in cold water than in hot water. This is called “reverse
solubility.” The water temperature will increase as recirculating water passes through
the cooling system. As a result, calcium and magnesium scales may form anywhere in
the system, but most likely on heated surfaces such as heat exchangers or surface
condensers. Silica will form in areas having the lowest water temperature, such as in
the cooling tower fill.
